name: Nonfarm Payrolls (Employment Situation report)
freq: Monthly, usually the first Friday of the month, 8:30 ET
what: The monthly change in the number of paid jobs in the US economy, excluding farm workers, private household employees and some non-profit staff. It comes from a survey of businesses and government agencies and is the broadest, most closely watched measure of US labour demand.
read: Compare the headline change with the forecast; a gap of tens of thousands of jobs is common and markets react to the surprise.
Revisions to the previous two months are published at the same time and can outweigh the new figure.
Read it together with the Unemployment Rate and Average Hourly Earnings released in the same report.
Strikes, weather and hiring for censuses or holidays can distort single months; the trend matters more.
market: Strong hiring suggests a firm economy and possibly higher Fed rates, which tends to lift the USD and Treasury yields.
Usually one of the largest scheduled movers of EUR/USD, USD/JPY, gold and US index futures.
Mixed reports (strong jobs, weak wages) can produce sharp moves in both directions within minutes.
When markets fear recession, a weak number can hurt stocks; when they fear inflation, a strong number can.

name: Unemployment Rate
freq: Monthly, with the Employment Situation report, usually the first Friday, 8:30 ET
what: The share of the labour force that is jobless and actively looking for work. It comes from a monthly survey of households, separate from the payroll survey of businesses, and is one of the two goals in the Fed's mandate (maximum employment).
read: Lower than forecast is the stronger result; it is reported to one decimal, so a 0.1-point surprise counts.
Rounding and survey noise make 0.1-point changes less reliable than a multi-month trend.
The participation rate in the same report explains whether a fall comes from hiring or from people leaving the labour force.
A rising trend from the recent low is often read as an early warning of a slowdown.
market: A lower rate signals a tight labour market and can support the USD through higher rate expectations.
A rising rate raises the odds of Fed cuts, which tends to weigh on the USD and push Treasury yields down.
It reacts in the same minute as Nonfarm Payrolls, so the combined picture drives the move.

name: Average Hourly Earnings
freq: Monthly, with the Employment Situation report, usually the first Friday, 8:30 ET
what: The average hourly pay of employees on private nonfarm payrolls. It is the most timely official gauge of US wage growth, which feeds into consumer spending and service-sector inflation.
read: The m/m figure is the headline on the calendar; 0.1 point above or below forecast is a meaningful surprise.
Changes in the mix of jobs can distort it: losing many low-paid jobs raises the average without anyone getting a raise.
The Employment Cost Index is a cleaner but quarterly measure of labour costs.
market: Faster wage growth suggests persistent inflation and a firmer Fed, which tends to support the USD and yields.
Slower wage growth can offset a strong payrolls figure and weaken the USD.
Wage surprises often matter most when the Fed is focused on inflation rather than jobs.

name: Initial Jobless Claims
source: US Department of Labor (Employment and Training Administration)
freq: Weekly, every Thursday, 8:30 ET (Wednesday in holiday weeks)
what: The number of people filing for unemployment insurance benefits for the first time during the past week. Because it is weekly and quick, it is the most timely signal of layoffs in the US economy.
read: Lower than forecast is the stronger result: fewer people are losing their jobs.
Weekly data are noisy (holidays, weather, seasonal adjustment); the 4-week average shows the trend better.
Continuing claims, in the same release, show whether people who lost jobs are finding new ones.
The week that contains the 12th of the month is the survey week for the monthly jobs report.
market: A sustained rise in claims points to a cooling labour market and can weigh on the USD and yields.
Usually a moderate mover; reactions grow when the market is worried about the labour market.
It is often released at the same time as other 8:30 ET data, which can dominate the reaction.

name: ADP National Employment Report
source: ADP Research (with Stanford Digital Economy Lab)
freq: Monthly, usually the Wednesday before the official jobs report, 8:15 ET
what: The monthly change in private-sector employment, estimated from ADP's anonymised payroll data covering millions of US workers. It is a private alternative to the official payrolls figure and is published two days earlier.
read: Compare with the forecast; the gap with the official Nonfarm Payrolls figure can be large in any month.
It covers only private employers, not government.
ADP changed its methodology in 2022; it is best read as an independent view of hiring, not a forecast of the official number.
ADP also publishes a weekly estimate (rated Low on the calendar).
market: A strong figure can lift the USD and yields as a preview of labour strength.
Moves are usually smaller than for the official report and can reverse when the official data come out.
It matters more when official data are delayed or missing.

name: Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS)
freq: Monthly, about five weeks after the reference month, 10:00 ET
what: The number of unfilled job positions on the last business day of the month, with hires, quits and layoffs. It measures labour demand and how easily workers can change jobs, which the Fed watches for wage pressure.
read: Higher openings than forecast signal stronger demand for workers.
The data are a month older than the jobs report, and revisions can be large.
The quits rate is a useful wage-pressure signal: workers quit more when they expect better pay elsewhere.
The ratio of openings to unemployed people summarises labour-market tightness.
market: More openings suggest a tight labour market and possibly higher rates, which can support the USD.
A sharp drop can raise expectations of Fed easing and weaken the USD and yields.
Reaction is usually moderate, larger when the Fed is focused on the labour market.

name: Employment Cost Index
freq: Quarterly, about a month after the quarter ends, 8:30 ET
what: The change in employers' total cost of labour per hour, covering wages, salaries and benefits. It holds the mix of jobs fixed, so it is a cleaner measure of labour-cost inflation than average hourly earnings.
read: Higher than forecast points to stronger labour-cost inflation.
Because it adjusts for job mix, it is less distorted by shifts between high- and low-paid sectors.
The Fed has cited it as a preferred measure of wage growth.
market: Faster labour-cost growth suggests persistent inflation and higher rate expectations, supporting the USD.
Moves are usually moderate, as it is often released alongside other data such as GDP or PCE.

name: Productivity and Costs
freq: Quarterly: preliminary about five weeks after the quarter ends, revised a month later, 8:30 ET
what: Productivity is output per hour worked in the nonfarm business sector; unit labour costs are what businesses pay in labour per unit of output. Together they show whether wage growth is inflationary or covered by higher efficiency.
read: Annualised figures; quarters are volatile and heavily revised with GDP.
Rising unit labour costs are an inflation signal; rising productivity lets wages grow without inflation.
The preliminary release usually matters more than the revision.
market: Higher labour costs can lift rate expectations and the USD; strong productivity is positive for growth and equities.
Usually a modest market mover.

name: Consumer Price Index
freq: Monthly, usually 10–15 days after the month ends, 8:30 ET
what: The change in prices of a basket of goods and services bought by urban consumers. Core CPI excludes food and energy, whose prices swing sharply. It is the most closely watched US inflation figure and shapes expectations for Fed policy.
read: Core CPI m/m is usually the version markets react to most; a 0.1-point surprise is large.
Headline y/y is the number quoted in the news; m/m shows the latest momentum.
Shelter (housing costs) is the biggest component and changes slowly.
CPI is not revised monthly (only seasonal factors annually), so the surprise stands.
market: Higher inflation raises expectations of a tighter Fed, lifting Treasury yields and usually the USD.
One of the largest scheduled movers of the USD, gold and US stock indices.
Hot inflation is usually negative for stocks and gold, as higher yields compete with them.
The Fed targets PCE inflation, but CPI arrives earlier and drives the first reaction.

name: Producer Price Index (final demand)
freq: Monthly, usually around the middle of the month, near CPI, 8:30 ET
what: The change in prices received by US producers for goods, services and construction sold to final demand. Core PPI excludes food and energy. It measures inflation at the wholesale stage, which can pass through to consumer prices.
read: Compare with forecast; core is less volatile and usually more informative.
Some PPI components (airfares, healthcare, portfolio management) feed the Fed's preferred PCE inflation measure, so analysts use PPI to update PCE forecasts.
It is usually less important than CPI, unless it comes first or the surprise is large.
Past months are revised.
market: Higher producer prices suggest future inflation pressure, which can lift yields and the USD.
The reaction tends to be smaller than for CPI, but can be large when PPI is released before CPI.
Trade margins swing a lot, so a surprise can come from margins rather than costs.

name: Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index
freq: Monthly, usually near the end of the following month, 8:30 ET (with Personal Income and Outlays)
what: The change in prices of goods and services consumed by households, from the GDP accounts. The Fed's 2% inflation target is defined on the PCE price index, and core PCE (excluding food and energy) is its key gauge of underlying inflation.
read: Core PCE m/m is the figure markets watch; a 0.1-point surprise is significant.
Because CPI and PPI come out earlier, the result is often well forecast, so surprises tend to be small.
It covers a broader basket than CPI and gives less weight to housing.
Earlier months are revised.
market: Higher inflation raises expectations of a tighter Fed, supporting the USD and yields.
Reaction is often smaller than for CPI because analysts can estimate it from CPI and PPI.
A surprise matters most close to a Fed meeting, as it is the Fed's target measure.

name: Personal Income and Outlays
freq: Monthly, usually near the end of the following month, 8:30 ET (with the PCE price index)
what: Personal spending is the change in households' consumption of goods and services; personal income is the change in all income received (wages, interest, transfers). Consumer spending is about two thirds of US GDP.
read: Higher spending than forecast signals stronger consumer demand.
Spending is in current dollars; compare with the PCE price index to separate volume from price.
Income versus spending shows the saving rate, which indicates how long spending can continue.
market: Strong spending supports growth and rate expectations, and can help the USD.
Usually overshadowed by the core PCE figure released at the same time.

name: University of Michigan Inflation Expectations
source: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers
freq: Monthly: preliminary around mid-month, final at month end, on a Friday, 10:00 ET
what: The median price increase US consumers expect over the next 12 months (the calendar figure) and the next 5–10 years, from the University of Michigan consumer survey. The Fed watches expectations because they can make inflation self-fulfilling.
read: Higher than forecast means consumers expect more inflation.
The 5–10 year expectation matters more to the Fed than the 1-year figure, which follows petrol and food prices.
The preliminary figure is based on a smaller sample and can be revised notably.
market: Rising expectations can lift yields and the USD by raising the odds of a firmer Fed.
Usually a moderate mover; it can matter more when the Fed cites expectations in its communication.

name: Gross Domestic Product
freq: Quarterly: advance estimate about 30 days after the quarter ends, second (Prelim) a month later, third (Final) a month after that, 8:30 ET
what: The change in the inflation-adjusted value of all goods and services produced in the US, expressed as an annualised quarterly rate. It is the broadest measure of economic activity.
read: The Advance estimate moves markets most; Prelim and Final revisions usually move less.
US GDP is annualised: a 2% figure means about 0.5% growth in that quarter.
Net exports and inventories can swing the headline; final sales to private domestic purchasers show underlying demand.
Much of the result is anticipated from monthly data, so surprises are often small.
market: Stronger growth supports rate expectations and the USD; weak growth raises the odds of easing.
Reaction depends on composition: a jump driven by inventories is discounted.
The price index and core PCE for the quarter, released at the same time, can drive the reaction instead.

name: GDP Price Index (deflator)
freq: Quarterly, with each GDP estimate, 8:30 ET
what: The change in prices of all goods and services included in GDP, annualised. It is the broadest measure of inflation in the economy, covering investment and government as well as consumers.
read: Higher than forecast indicates more inflation in the quarter.
Quarterly core PCE, released at the same time, is usually more relevant to the Fed.
Like GDP, it is revised in the Prelim and Final estimates.
market: Higher inflation can lift yields and the USD; usually overshadowed by headline GDP.
Matters more when inflation is the market's main focus.

name: Advance Monthly Retail Sales
freq: Monthly, around the 15th, for the previous month, 8:30 ET
what: The change in the dollar value of sales at retailers and food-service businesses. Core Retail Sales excludes automobiles, whose sales are volatile. It is the earliest monthly view of US consumer spending.
read: Figures are in current dollars, not adjusted for inflation: high inflation inflates sales.
Core (ex autos) and the control group (which feeds GDP) show underlying demand better than the headline.
Previous months are revised and can change the picture.
Petrol prices move the headline through gasoline-station sales.
market: Strong sales suggest resilient consumers and firmer rates, which tends to support the USD and yields.
Often a major mover of USD pairs, especially when the consumer is the focus.
Weak sales can lower rate expectations and weigh on the USD.

name: Advance Durable Goods Orders
freq: Monthly, around the 25th, for the previous month, 8:30 ET
what: The change in new orders placed with US manufacturers for goods expected to last at least three years. Core excludes transportation, because aircraft orders swing the headline wildly.
read: The headline is very volatile because of aircraft orders; Core is more informative.
Analysts also watch non-defence capital goods ex aircraft as a gauge of business investment.
Revisions in the full factory orders report can be large.
market: Strong orders point to business investment and growth, which can support the USD.
The market often ignores headline swings caused by aircraft orders.
Usually a moderate mover.

name: Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization
freq: Monthly, around the middle of the month, 9:15 ET
what: The change in inflation-adjusted output of US factories, mines and utilities, with capacity utilisation (the share of production capacity in use). Manufacturing is the main component.
read: Utilities output swings with weather, so manufacturing output is the cleaner signal.
Capacity utilisation near its long-run high can signal inflation pressure.
Previous months are revised.
market: Stronger output supports growth expectations and the USD; usually a small mover.
Data are often anticipated by earlier surveys like ISM and regional Fed indices.

name: US International Trade in Goods and Services
source: US Census Bureau and Bureau of Economic Analysis
freq: Monthly, about five weeks after the month ends, 8:30 ET
what: The difference between the value of US exports and imports of goods and services. The US runs a persistent deficit, so the figure is negative; a smaller deficit counts as an improvement.
read: A smaller deficit (less negative) than forecast is the stronger result.
An advance goods-only estimate is published earlier, so surprises are often small.
Tariffs and stock-building before tariffs can cause large one-off swings.
market: A narrower deficit adds to GDP and can mildly support the USD.
Usually a small mover, unless trade policy is in focus.

name: ISM Manufacturing PMI
freq: Monthly, first business day of the month, 10:00 ET
what: A diffusion index from a survey of purchasing managers at US manufacturers, covering new orders, production, employment, deliveries and inventories. It is one of the earliest monthly readings of the US factory sector.
read: 50 is the dividing line: above 50 means activity is expanding, below 50 contracting.
Distance from 50 shows breadth, not size; a reading of 48 is mild contraction.
New Orders shows future activity; Employment previews factory jobs; Prices Paid is an inflation signal.
Data are not revised, apart from annual seasonal adjustments.
market: A stronger reading points to growth and can support the USD and yields.
A move across 50 often attracts more attention than the size of the surprise.
Manufacturing is a small share of US GDP, but the timing makes this survey market-moving.

name: ISM Services PMI
freq: Monthly, third business day of the month, 10:00 ET
what: A diffusion index from a survey of purchasing managers at US service businesses, which make up most of the economy. It covers business activity, new orders, employment and supplier deliveries.
read: 50 is the dividing line between expansion and contraction.
Business Activity and New Orders show demand; the Prices index tracks service-sector inflation.
It used to be called the ISM Non-Manufacturing PMI.
Not revised, apart from annual seasonal adjustments.
market: A stronger reading supports growth and rate expectations, and the USD.
Because services dominate the US economy, a surprise below 50 can move markets strongly.
The Prices sub-index can drive the reaction when inflation is in focus.

name: ISM Prices Paid indices
freq: Monthly, with the ISM Manufacturing (first business day) and Services (third business day) reports, 10:00 ET
what: The prices sub-index of the ISM surveys: the share of purchasing managers reporting higher prices for inputs minus those reporting lower prices, as a diffusion index. It is an early signal of cost pressure.
read: Above 50 means more firms report rising prices than falling prices.
It shows how widespread price increases are, not how large they are.
Read it alongside CPI and PPI as an early indicator.
market: Higher readings can lift inflation and rate expectations, supporting the USD and yields.
Usually secondary to the headline PMI, but can lead the reaction when inflation is the focus.

name: S&P Global US Manufacturing and Services PMI
freq: Monthly: flash estimate in the last week of the month, final early the next month, 9:45 ET
what: Purchasing managers' indices from S&P Global surveys of US manufacturers and service providers. The flash release, based on most of the responses, comes before month end and is the earliest monthly read of US business activity.
read: 50 separates expansion from contraction.
The flash estimate matters more; the final usually differs only slightly.
Readings can differ from the ISM surveys, which use different samples and weights.
market: A stronger reading supports growth expectations and the USD.
Usually a smaller mover than ISM, whose data are older but more established.
Comments on prices and hiring in the release can be informative.

name: Empire State Manufacturing Survey
source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
freq: Monthly, around the 15th, 8:30 ET
what: A survey of manufacturers in New York State on business conditions. The headline is the share reporting improving conditions minus the share reporting worse. It is the earliest regional factory survey each month.
read: 0 is the dividing line: positive means conditions are improving, negative deteriorating.
It is volatile, with swings of 10–20 points not unusual; small samples cause noise.
Prices, new orders and six-month expectations offer extra detail.
market: A stronger reading can support the USD as an early hint for the ISM survey.
Usually a moderate mover; large surprises attract more attention.

name: Philadelphia Fed Manufacturing Business Outlook Survey
freq: Monthly, usually the third Thursday, 8:30 ET
what: A survey of manufacturers in the Philadelphia Fed district (Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware). The headline is the share of firms reporting increased activity minus the share reporting a decrease.
read: 0 is the dividing line between expanding and contracting activity.
Volatile month to month; trends and sub-indices (new orders, prices paid) add context.
It is one of the earliest signals for the national ISM survey.
market: A stronger reading can support the USD as a growth signal.
Usually a moderate mover, often released with jobless claims.

name: Richmond Fed Fifth District Survey of Manufacturing Activity
freq: Monthly, usually the fourth Tuesday, 10:00 ET
what: A survey of manufacturers in the Richmond Fed district (mid-Atlantic and southeast). The composite index combines shipments, new orders and employment.
read: 0 separates expansion from contraction.
Small sample and volatile; trends matter more than single months.
market: A stronger reading can slightly support the USD; usually a small mover.

name: Chicago Business Barometer (Chicago PMI)
freq: Monthly, last business day of the month, 9:45 ET
what: A survey of businesses in the Chicago region on production, orders, employment, deliveries and inventories. It covers both manufacturing and non-manufacturing firms and is published just before the national ISM survey.
read: 50 separates expansion from contraction.
Volatile; it is read as a hint for the ISM Manufacturing PMI the next day.
market: A stronger reading can support the USD; usually a modest mover, larger on big surprises.

name: Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index
freq: Monthly, last Tuesday of the month, 10:00 ET
what: An index of US consumers' views on current business and job conditions and their expectations for the next six months, from a monthly survey. 1985 = 100. It signals how willing households are to spend.
read: Higher than forecast means consumers are more optimistic.
It leans towards labour-market conditions; the jobs plentiful minus jobs hard to get gap is watched as a labour signal.
The previous month is often revised.
market: Rising confidence supports spending expectations and can lift the USD.
Usually a moderate mover; reaction is larger when consumer health is in focus.

name: University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index
source: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers
freq: Monthly: preliminary around mid-month, final at month end, on a Friday, 10:00 ET
what: An index of US consumers' attitudes about personal finances, business conditions and buying conditions, from a survey. 1966 = 100. The same survey produces the inflation expectations figures.
read: Higher than forecast means consumers are more optimistic.
It is more sensitive to prices, interest rates and politics than the Conference Board index.
The preliminary figure usually matters more than the revision.
market: Higher sentiment can support the USD by pointing to stronger spending.
Often the inflation expectations in the same release move markets more than the sentiment index.

name: New Residential Construction (Building Permits, Housing Starts)
freq: Monthly, around the 17th, 8:30 ET
what: Building permits are the number of new homes authorised by local permit offices; housing starts are the number of new homes on which construction began. Both are annualised totals. Permits lead starts and are a forward indicator of construction activity.
read: Figures are annualised, in millions of units; compare with forecast.
Multi-family units swing the totals; single-family figures show the trend better.
Starts are weather-sensitive; permits are smoother.
Previous months are revised.
market: Stronger construction points to growth and can mildly support the USD.
Housing is very sensitive to mortgage rates, so it shows how Fed policy is affecting the economy.
Usually a small to moderate mover.

name: New Residential Sales
freq: Monthly, around the 25th, 10:00 ET
what: The annualised number of newly built single-family homes sold during the month. It is recorded when contracts are signed, so it reacts quickly to changes in mortgage rates and demand.
read: Annualised figure; large revisions and wide margins of error are normal.
Inventory and median prices in the same report add context.
market: Stronger sales point to housing demand and can mildly support the USD; usually a small mover.

name: Existing-Home Sales
freq: Monthly, around the 20th–25th, 10:00 ET
what: The annualised number of previously owned homes (single-family, townhouses, condos, co-ops) sold during the month. It counts closings, so it reflects contracts signed one to two months earlier.
read: Annualised figure in millions; compare with forecast.
Pending Home Sales gives an earlier signal of this figure.
Inventory and median price show supply conditions.
market: Stronger sales can mildly support the USD; usually a small mover.

name: Pending Home Sales Index
freq: Monthly, near the end of the month, 10:00 ET
what: The change in the number of contracts signed to buy existing homes. Because contracts close one to two months later, it is a leading indicator for existing home sales.
read: m/m change in percent; volatile month to month.
Strong pending sales usually mean stronger existing home sales later.
market: Stronger readings can mildly support the USD; usually a small mover.

name: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report (crude oil stocks)
freq: Weekly, Wednesday, 10:30 ET (delayed a day in holiday weeks)
what: The weekly change in the number of barrels of crude oil held in US commercial inventories, excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It reflects the balance between US production, imports and refinery demand.
read: A smaller build or larger draw than forecast means tighter supply, which tends to lift oil prices.
Gasoline and distillate stocks, refinery utilisation and Cushing stocks in the same report also matter.
The private API report on Tuesday evening often sets expectations.
market: The main reaction is in crude oil (WTI, Brent) and energy stocks, not the USD.
Oil-linked currencies such as CAD and NOK can move with oil prices.
The link to the USD is indirect and not stable.

name: US Treasury note and bond auctions
freq: Monthly for each maturity, on dates set by the Treasury auction schedule; results at 1:00 ET
what: The Treasury sells government debt at auctions. The calendar shows the high yield accepted at the auction; the bid-to-cover ratio and the share bought by foreign and domestic investors show how strong demand was.
read: Compare the auction yield with the yield trading just before the auction (when-issued): an auction above it ('tail') signals weak demand.
Bid-to-cover above recent averages signals strong demand.
Weak demand at long maturities can push yields up across the curve.
market: A weak auction lifts yields; this can support the USD against low-yielders like the JPY but weigh on stocks.
Reactions are usually small, but matter more when fiscal deficits or Treasury demand are in focus.

name: Federal Funds Target Range (FOMC rate decision)
freq: Eight scheduled meetings a year, decision at 2:00 ET on the second day
what: The target range for the overnight rate at which banks lend reserves to each other, set by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). It is the Fed's main policy tool and the anchor for US interest rates.
read: The decision is usually well anticipated through futures markets; a surprise versus pricing is rare and powerful.
The calendar shows the upper bound of the range.
The vote split and any dissents show how divided the committee is.
The statement, projections and press conference often matter more than the decision itself.
market: A higher-than-expected rate, or a pause when a cut was expected, tends to lift the USD and yields.
It moves every USD pair, gold, Treasury yields and US stocks.
The first reaction can reverse during the press conference.

name: FOMC Statement
freq: After each of the eight scheduled meetings, 2:00 ET
what: The short official statement announcing the rate decision, the committee's view of the economy and inflation, and any guidance on future policy. Traders compare it word by word with the previous statement.
read: Look for changed wording about inflation, the labour market and the outlook for policy.
Dissenting votes are listed at the end.
There is no forecast, so the reaction depends on how the wording differs from expectations.
market: A more hawkish tone (concern about inflation) tends to lift the USD and yields; a dovish tone weakens them.
Released together with the rate decision, so both drive the move in the first minutes.

name: FOMC Press Conference
freq: After each of the eight scheduled meetings, 2:30 ET
what: The Fed Chair explains the decision and answers journalists' questions for about an hour. It is the main channel for nuance about future policy.
read: There is no number: markets react to the Chair's tone and answers about future rate moves.
Watch answers on the timing of the next move, inflation risks and the balance sheet.
market: Hawkish remarks tend to support the USD and yields; dovish remarks weaken them.
Volatility can be high for the full hour, and the reaction to the statement can reverse.

name: Summary of Economic Projections (dot plot)
freq: Four times a year (March, June, September, December meetings), 2:00 ET
what: FOMC participants' projections for growth, unemployment, inflation and the appropriate path of the policy rate. The 'dot plot' shows each participant's view of where rates should be at the end of each year.
read: Compare the median dot for each year with what markets price for rates.
Projections are not commitments; they change with data.
Changes from the previous projections matter more than the levels.
market: Higher rate dots than expected tend to lift the USD and short-term yields.
Released with the statement, so the effects combine.

name: Minutes of the FOMC Meeting
freq: Three weeks after each scheduled meeting, 2:00 ET
what: The detailed record of the discussion at the last FOMC meeting, without names. It shows the range of views, the risks members debated and how much support there was for different policy options.
read: No forecast: read for how many participants favoured tighter or looser policy ('many', 'some', 'a few').
Can be outdated if data since the meeting have changed the outlook.
market: Hawkish details can lift the USD and yields; dovish ones weaken them.
Usually a moderate mover; larger when the meeting was closely balanced.

name: Beige Book (Summary of Commentary on Current Economic Conditions)
freq: Eight times a year, about two weeks before each FOMC meeting, 2:00 ET
what: A report compiling anecdotal information on economic conditions from businesses and contacts in each of the twelve Federal Reserve districts. It is one of the inputs for FOMC discussions.
read: Qualitative only: look at how many districts report growth, decline or price pressure.
Compare tone with the previous edition.
market: Usually a small mover; a clearly weaker or stronger tone can affect rate expectations and the USD.

name: Fed Chair speeches and testimony
freq: Irregular; includes semi-annual Monetary Policy Report testimony to Congress and the Jackson Hole symposium in August
what: Public remarks by the Chair of the Federal Reserve Board, who leads the FOMC. Speeches, interviews and testimony before Congress are the Chair's main way of guiding expectations between meetings.
read: No number: markets look for hints about the next rate decision and the Fed's view of inflation and jobs.
Prepared text is often released at the start; the question-and-answer part can move markets more.
Testimony usually lasts two days (one in each chamber of Congress).
market: Hawkish remarks tend to lift the USD and yields; dovish remarks weaken them.
One of the most market-moving speakers in the world; reactions spread to gold, stocks and all USD pairs.

name: FOMC member speeches
source: Federal Reserve Board and regional Federal Reserve Banks
freq: Irregular; frequent, except during the blackout period around each FOMC meeting
what: Speeches, interviews and testimony by Fed Governors and regional Fed Bank presidents. Voting members for the current year carry more weight; the New York Fed president votes permanently.
read: No number: look for views on the next rate decision that differ from market pricing.
Members known as hawks or doves matter most when they change their stance.
No Fed officials speak on policy in the blackout period before and right after each meeting.
market: Hawkish remarks can lift the USD and yields; dovish remarks can weaken them.
The calendar rates most such speeches Low; it rates Medium those by influential members such as governors.
Reactions are usually smaller than for the Chair.

name: Treasury Secretary speeches
freq: Irregular
what: Public remarks by the US Treasury Secretary, who manages federal debt, speaks for the government on the dollar and leads trade and sanctions negotiations with other countries.
read: No number: watch remarks on the dollar, tariffs, debt issuance and the Fed.
Comments on the dollar's level are rare and therefore notable.
market: Comments on trade, tariffs or the dollar can move the USD and the currencies of trading partners (CNY, JPY, MXN, CAD, EUR).
Signals about long-term debt issuance can move Treasury yields.

name: US President speeches
freq: Irregular
what: Public remarks by the US President. Statements about tariffs, trade deals, fiscal policy, the Federal Reserve or geopolitics can affect markets.
read: No number: markets react to new policy information, such as tariff announcements or comments on the Fed.
The rating on the calendar reflects expected market relevance, not the event's political importance.
market: Tariff or trade news can move the USD, trading-partner currencies and stocks sharply.
Comments on the Fed or interest rates can move yields and the USD.
Direction depends entirely on content; there is no standard reaction.

name: ECB Interest Rate Decision and Monetary Policy Statement
freq: Eight times a year, about every six weeks; decision published at 14:15 CET
what: The ECB Governing Council sets the euro area's three key interest rates: the deposit facility rate, the main refinancing rate and the marginal lending rate. Its aim is inflation of 2% over the medium term. Since September 2024 the ECB steers its stance through the deposit facility rate, with the main refinancing rate set slightly above it. The written Monetary Policy Statement explains the decision.
read: The rate change itself is usually fully expected; the surprise, if any, is in the size or in a decision markets did not price.
The Statement's wording on future steps (data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting, risks to inflation) often matters more than the rate.
Watch changes to the balance-sheet programmes and any revision to the staff inflation and growth projections (March, June, September, December).
Compare the decision with market pricing, not only with the consensus forecast.
market: A higher rate or a more hawkish tone raises euro yields and tends to strengthen the euro; a cut or a dovish tone tends to weaken it.
EUR/USD, EUR/GBP, EUR/JPY and EUR/CHF react first, together with Bund yields and European equity indices.
An expected cut paired with a signal that cuts are over can lift the euro, the opposite of the headline move.
Volatility often continues into the press conference 30 minutes later.

name: ECB Press Conference
freq: After each monetary policy meeting, at 14:45 CET
what: The ECB President and Vice-President explain the rate decision, read the introductory statement and answer journalists' questions. It is the main place where the ECB gives guidance on what it may do next and how it sees inflation, growth and risks.
read: Listen for guidance on the next meetings and whether further moves are open, likely or ruled out.
Answers in the Q&A can contradict or soften the written statement; markets react to unscripted remarks.
Mentions of how unanimous the decision was show how divided the Governing Council is.
Comments on the euro exchange rate are rare but can move the currency directly.
market: A tone that implies higher rates for longer tends to support the euro; hints of more easing tend to weigh on it.
EUR pairs and euro-area bond yields can swing in both directions during the hour as answers come in.
The move after the press conference can reverse the reaction to the decision published 30 minutes earlier.

name: Account of the ECB Monetary Policy Meeting
freq: About four weeks after each monetary policy meeting, usually at 13:30 CET
what: A summary of the Governing Council's discussion at the previous policy meeting, without naming individual members. It shows the arguments behind the decision and how wide the range of views was.
read: Look for how many members favoured a different decision or a different pace.
Phrases about inflation risks being up or down show which way the debate leans.
Because it describes a meeting weeks ago, newer data or speeches can make it stale.
market: Accounts that sound more hawkish than the press conference can lift the euro; more dovish accounts can weigh on it.
The reaction is usually smaller than on decision day and fades if newer data contradict it.

name: ECB President speech or testimony
freq: Irregular; speeches, panels, interviews and hearings at the European Parliament
what: Public remarks by the ECB President, currently Christine Lagarde. As head of the Governing Council her view carries the most weight, so her comments between meetings can change expectations for the next decision.
read: Check whether the event is about monetary policy; many speeches cover other topics and pass without effect.
New views on inflation, growth or the next rate move matter most; repeating the last statement usually does not.
Q&A sessions and hearings carry more risk of unscripted comments than prepared texts.
market: Remarks pointing to higher or longer-held rates tend to support the euro; hints of easing tend to weaken it.
EUR/USD and euro-area yields react most; the effect is larger shortly before a policy meeting.
If the remarks only confirm market pricing there is often little or no reaction.

name: Speeches by ECB Executive Board and Governing Council members
source: European Central Bank and national central banks of the euro area
freq: Irregular; several each week
what: Speeches and interviews by ECB Executive Board members (such as the Vice-President and the Chief Economist) and national central bank governors who vote on the Governing Council, such as the Bundesbank President. They show how individual policymakers lean before the next decision.
read: Know whether the speaker usually leans hawkish or dovish; a change from their usual stance is the real news.
Remarks by the Chief Economist and the largest national central banks tend to carry more weight.
One member's view is not the decision; look for several officials saying the same thing.
market: Hawkish comments (worry about inflation, no rush to cut) tend to support the euro; dovish ones tend to weigh on it.
Effects are usually small and short-lived unless the remarks shift pricing for the next meeting.
During the quiet period in the week before a policy meeting officials do not discuss policy.

name: Euro Area Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP)
freq: Monthly; flash estimate on the last working day of the month or early in the next, final about mid-month after; 11:00 CET
what: The HICP measures the change in prices consumers pay for goods and services across the euro area, using the same method in every member state. It is the inflation measure behind the ECB's 2% target. Core excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco to show underlying price pressure.
read: The flash estimate moves markets; the final release rarely differs and usually passes quietly.
Core and services inflation are watched closely because they show persistent pressure the ECB cares about.
National releases (German, French, Spanish, Italian) earlier in the week often signal the euro area figure in advance.
Compare with the 2% target and with the ECB staff projections.
market: Higher inflation than expected raises expectations of tighter ECB policy and tends to strengthen the euro.
Lower inflation than expected tends to raise expectations of cuts and weaken the euro.
EUR/USD, euro-area short-term yields and Bund futures react most.
If national data already showed the surprise, the euro area release can bring little reaction.

name: German Consumer Price Index
freq: Monthly; preliminary figure near the end of the month (usually 14:00 CET), final about two weeks later
what: Measures the change in prices of goods and services bought by households in Germany, the largest euro-area economy. Several federal states publish their own figures on the morning of the national release, which hint at the result. Destatis also publishes the harmonised (HICP) rate that feeds the euro area figure.
read: The preliminary release matters; the final rarely changes it.
State figures (such as North Rhine-Westphalia and Bavaria) published earlier the same day often reveal the direction.
Monthly changes can be noisy because of energy and seasonal items such as package holidays.
Markets compare it with the forecast and use it to adjust the expected euro area flash estimate.
market: Higher than expected German inflation tends to strengthen the euro by raising expectations of tighter ECB policy.
Lower than expected readings tend to weaken the euro.
EUR/USD and Bund yields react; the effect is larger when the euro area flash release is days away.

name: French, Spanish and Italian consumer prices
freq: Monthly; preliminary or flash figures around the end of the month, finals about two weeks later
what: The preliminary consumer price indices of the second, third and fourth largest euro-area economies. They come out in the days before the euro area flash estimate and together with Germany cover most of the euro area basket.
read: The preliminary or flash release matters; the final is rarely revised much.
Spain's flash figure usually comes first and is the earliest hint of the month's euro area trend.
Look at whether all national releases point the same way before drawing conclusions.
market: Higher than expected inflation tends to support the euro through higher ECB rate expectations; lower readings tend to weigh on it.
The reaction is usually smaller than for Germany or the euro area flash estimate.
National bond spreads and EUR/USD react most.

name: HCOB Flash Purchasing Managers' Index (euro area, Germany, France)
source: S&P Global and Hamburg Commercial Bank (HCOB)
freq: Monthly, about a week before the month ends; France 09:15, Germany 09:30, euro area 10:00 CET
what: A survey of purchasing managers at manufacturing and services companies about output, new orders, employment, prices and delivery times. The flash estimate is based on most of the month's responses and is the earliest picture of business activity for the current month.
read: 50 separates expansion (above) from contraction (below); the distance from 50 shows how strong the change is.
Compare with the forecast and with the previous month; direction matters as well as the level.
Services carry more weight for the economy; manufacturing is more sensitive to global trade.
Price sub-indices show cost pressure and can matter for the ECB.
market: Readings above forecast tend to support the euro and European equities; weak readings tend to weigh on them.
France reports first, so a surprise there can set the tone before Germany and the euro area.
EUR/USD often reacts within minutes; the effect is larger when growth is the market's main worry.

name: HCOB Final Purchasing Managers' Index
source: S&P Global and Hamburg Commercial Bank (HCOB)
freq: Monthly; manufacturing on the first working day of the month, services on the third, mornings CET
what: The complete monthly PMI surveys. For the euro area, Germany and France they confirm or revise the flash figures. Spain and Italy have no flash, so their releases are the first reading for those economies.
read: 50 is the line between expansion and contraction.
For the euro area, Germany and France the gap between final and flash matters; it is usually small.
Spanish and Italian PMIs are new information and are compared with their forecasts.
market: Upward revisions or strong Spanish and Italian readings can lift the euro slightly; weak ones can weigh on it.
Reactions are usually smaller than for the flash release.

name: ifo Business Climate Index for Germany
freq: Monthly, usually in the last full week of the month at 10:00 CET
what: Based on a monthly survey of around 9,000 German firms in manufacturing, services, trade and construction. Firms rate their current business situation and their expectations for the next six months. It is one of the most watched indicators of the German economy.
read: The headline Business Climate combines the current assessment and expectations; expectations are the forward-looking part.
Compare with the forecast and the previous month; several months in the same direction signal a turning point.
It is an index, not a growth rate: changes matter more than the level.
market: A stronger than expected reading tends to support the euro and German equities; a weaker one tends to weigh on them.
EUR/USD and the DAX react most.
When markets focus on inflation and the ECB, the reaction to ifo can be small.

name: ZEW Indicator of Economic Sentiment
source: ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research, Mannheim
freq: Monthly, usually on a Tuesday around the middle of the month at 11:00 CET
what: A survey of financial analysts and institutional investors about their expectations for the economy over the next six months, for Germany and the euro area. The result is a balance: the share of optimists minus the share of pessimists.
read: Positive values mean more analysts expect improvement than deterioration; negative values mean the opposite.
The German figure gets the most attention; the euro area figure comes at the same time.
It reflects financial market opinion and can swing sharply with share prices and news.
The separate current situation reading shows how analysts judge the present.
market: A higher than expected reading tends to support the euro; a lower one tends to weigh on it.
Because it comes before ifo and PMIs, a large surprise can shift expectations for those releases.
Reactions are often modest and short-lived.

name: GfK Consumer Climate (Germany)
source: GfK and NIM (Nuremberg Institute for Market Decisions)
freq: Monthly, near the end of the month, usually 08:00 CET
what: Based on a survey of about 2,000 German consumers about income expectations, economic expectations and willingness to buy and to save. The headline is a forecast of consumer sentiment for the following month.
read: Negative values have been common for years; the change from the previous month matters more than the sign.
A rising willingness to save usually means weaker consumer spending.
Compare with the forecast; surprises are usually small.
market: A better than expected reading can slightly support the euro; a weaker one can slightly weigh on it.
The effect is usually small because consumer spending data come later.

name: Euro Area Consumer Confidence (flash)
freq: Monthly, flash estimate around the 20th of the month at 16:00 CET
what: The European Commission's survey of households in the euro area about their financial situation, the general economy and plans for major purchases. The flash estimate comes before the full business and consumer survey at the end of the month.
read: It is a balance of positive minus negative answers; it is normally negative, so the change matters.
Compare with the forecast and the long-term average.
The final figure later in the month is usually very close.
market: A higher than expected reading can slightly support the euro; a lower one can slightly weigh on it.
Reactions are usually small; it matters more when consumer demand is in focus.

name: Sentix Investor Confidence (euro area)
freq: Monthly, on the first Monday of the month at 10:30 CET
what: A survey of private and institutional investors about the current situation and their expectations for the euro-area economy over six months. It is one of the first sentiment readings of each month.
read: It is a balance of positive minus negative answers; the change from the previous month matters.
It is driven by investors, so it follows market moves closely.
market: A better than expected reading can slightly support the euro; usually the reaction is small.

name: Euro Area Gross Domestic Product
freq: Quarterly; preliminary flash about 30 days after the quarter, flash about 45 days, revised about 65 days; 11:00 CET
what: GDP measures the total value of goods and services produced in the euro area. It is the broadest measure of economic growth. Eurostat publishes several estimates as more national data come in; employment change is published with the later estimates.
read: The q/q figure is the change from the previous quarter, not annualised.
The preliminary flash release matters most; later estimates rarely change it much.
Germany, France, Spain and Italy publish their own first estimates on or just before the same day, so much is known in advance.
Two consecutive negative quarters are often described as a technical recession.
market: Stronger growth than expected can support the euro by reducing pressure for rate cuts; weaker growth can weigh on it.
The reaction is often limited because national data reveal most of the result earlier.
EUR/USD and European equities react most.

name: German Gross Domestic Product
freq: Quarterly; first estimate about 30 days after the quarter, detailed result about 55 days after; 10:00 CET
what: The change in the total output of the German economy, which accounts for roughly a quarter of euro-area output. The detailed release adds the breakdown into consumption, investment and trade.
read: The preliminary figure matters most; the final is mostly a confirmation with revisions.
q/q is the change from the previous quarter, seasonally and calendar adjusted.
Revisions to earlier quarters can change the picture as much as the new number.
market: Higher than expected growth tends to support the euro and the DAX; weaker growth tends to weigh on them.
A German surprise often shifts expectations for the euro area figure released later.

name: French, Spanish and Italian Gross Domestic Product
freq: Quarterly; first estimates about 30 days after the quarter, mornings CET
what: First estimates of quarterly growth for France, Spain and Italy. They come out on or just before the day of the euro area preliminary flash GDP and together with Germany make up most of it.
read: q/q is the change from the previous quarter, not annualised.
Compare each with its forecast, then add them up mentally to judge the euro area release.
These first estimates can be revised later.
market: Better than expected growth can support the euro; weaker growth can weigh on it.
Reactions are usually smaller than for Germany; national bond spreads can react too.

name: German Unemployment (Federal Employment Agency)
freq: Monthly, around the end of the month or the first working days of the next, at 09:55 CET
what: The seasonally adjusted change in the number of registered unemployed people in Germany and the registered unemployment rate. It is the most timely official measure of the German labour market.
read: A negative change (fewer unemployed) is positive for the economy; ForexFactory treats a figure below forecast as good for the euro.
Changes are measured in thousands of people; compare with the forecast.
The rate moves slowly; the monthly change is what markets watch.
market: A smaller rise or a fall in unemployment versus forecast tends to support the euro; a larger rise tends to weigh on it.
The reaction is usually modest because inflation data dominate ECB expectations.

name: Euro Area Unemployment Rate
freq: Monthly, about one month after the reference month; 11:00 CET for the euro area
what: The share of the labour force in the euro area that is unemployed and looking for work, based on harmonised labour force definitions. Italy's national figure is published separately by Istat.
read: Lower than forecast is good for the currency.
The rate changes slowly, often by 0.1 point or not at all, so surprises are rare.
Past months are often revised.
market: A lower rate than expected can slightly support the euro; a higher one can slightly weigh on it.
Reactions are usually small; a tight labour market matters through wage and services inflation.

name: German Manufacturing Orders
freq: Monthly, about five weeks after the month ends, at 08:00 CET
what: The change in the value of new orders received by German manufacturers, adjusted for prices, seasons and calendar effects. Orders lead production, so they show where German industry is heading.
read: Large single orders (for example aircraft or ships) can make the monthly number swing; Destatis also reports orders excluding them.
Look at domestic versus foreign orders for the source of demand.
A trend over several months says more than one month.
market: Better than expected orders can support the euro and German industrial shares; weaker orders can weigh on them.
Reactions are usually small because the data are volatile.

name: Industrial Production (Germany, euro area and member states)
freq: Monthly; German figure about five to six weeks after the month (08:00 CET), euro area about six weeks after (11:00 CET)
what: The change in the volume of output from manufacturing, mining, energy and (for Germany) construction. It shows how much industry is actually producing and feeds into quarterly GDP.
read: Monthly changes are volatile; energy-intensive sectors and car production often drive swings.
National releases come before the euro area figure, which is therefore rarely a big surprise.
Revisions to the previous month can be large.
market: Better than expected output can support the euro; weaker output can weigh on it.
Reactions are usually small, larger for Germany than for the euro area aggregate.

name: Retail Sales (Germany and euro area)
freq: Monthly; German figure about four weeks after the month (08:00 CET), euro area about five weeks after (11:00 CET)
what: The change in the volume of sales by retailers, adjusted for prices and seasons. It is a direct gauge of household spending, the largest part of the economy.
read: German retail sales are volatile and often revised; one month says little.
The euro area figure is published after most national data, so it rarely surprises much.
Compare with the forecast and the previous month's revision.
market: Stronger sales than expected can support the euro; weaker sales can weigh on it.
Reactions are usually small.

name: National and European elections
source: Electoral authorities of the member states and the EU
freq: Irregular; on the election day, results usually come in overnight or over the weekend
what: Parliamentary, presidential or European Parliament elections in euro-area countries. Results can change fiscal policy, EU cooperation and the risk premium investors demand on government bonds.
read: There is no forecast; compare the result with polls and with what markets expected.
Results that make coalition-building hard or favour parties critical of the EU raise uncertainty.
The market reaction often shows at the next market open after the vote.
market: Results seen as raising political or fiscal risk tend to weaken the euro and widen bond spreads.
Results seen as stable can lift the euro, sometimes with a gap at the weekly open.
French and Italian bond spreads versus Germany are a common gauge of the risk.

name: SNB Policy Rate and Monetary Policy Assessment
freq: Quarterly (March, June, September, December); decision at 09:30 CET
what: The Swiss National Bank sets the SNB policy rate and explains it in its Monetary Policy Assessment, which includes a new conditional inflation forecast. The SNB defines price stability as annual CPI inflation below 2%. Besides the rate, it can intervene in the foreign exchange market.
read: Compare the rate with the forecast and with market pricing; with only four meetings a year each one carries weight.
The conditional inflation forecast shows where the SNB expects inflation to go if the rate stays unchanged.
Wording on willingness to intervene in the foreign exchange market matters as much as the rate.
Mentions of the franc being highly valued signal concern about franc strength.
market: A higher rate or less willingness to sell francs tends to strengthen the franc; a cut or stronger intervention language tends to weaken it.
EUR/CHF and USD/CHF react most; Swiss government bond yields too.
The franc is also a safe-haven currency, so global risk mood can outweigh the decision.

name: SNB Press Conference
freq: Quarterly, after each monetary policy assessment, at 10:00 CET
what: The SNB Governing Board explains the decision and answers questions. It is the main chance to hear how the SNB views inflation, the franc and the possibility of negative rates or currency interventions.
read: Listen for comments on future rate moves, including whether negative rates are possible.
Remarks on foreign exchange interventions and the franc's value are key for the currency.
Answers can soften or sharpen the written assessment published 30 minutes earlier.
market: Hawkish remarks or less readiness to intervene tend to strengthen the franc; dovish remarks tend to weaken it.
EUR/CHF and USD/CHF can move again after the initial reaction to the decision.

name: Speeches by SNB officials
freq: Irregular
what: Speeches and interviews by members of the SNB Governing Board, led by Chairman Martin Schlegel since October 2024. Between the four yearly decisions they are the main signal of the SNB's thinking.
read: Look for new comments on inflation, the rate path, negative rates and foreign exchange interventions.
The Chairman's remarks carry the most weight.
Repetition of the last assessment usually causes little reaction.
market: Signals of easier policy or more intervention tend to weaken the franc; hawkish signals tend to strengthen it.
EUR/CHF and USD/CHF react most.

name: Swiss Consumer Price Index
freq: Monthly, in the first days of the following month, at 08:30 CET
what: Measures the change in prices of goods and services bought by households in Switzerland. The SNB treats annual CPI inflation below 2% as price stability, so this is the key input for its decisions.
read: The y/y rate is compared with the SNB's 0–2% range and its latest conditional forecast.
The FSO also publishes core inflation, excluding fresh and seasonal products, energy and fuel.
Imported prices are sensitive to the franc's exchange rate; domestic prices show home-grown pressure.
Swiss inflation is low, so a surprise of 0.1 point can matter.
market: Higher inflation than expected lowers the chance of SNB rate cuts and tends to strengthen the franc.
Lower inflation than expected raises the chance of cuts or negative rates and tends to weaken it.
EUR/CHF and USD/CHF react most.

name: Swiss Gross Domestic Product
freq: Quarterly, about two months after the quarter ends, in the morning CET
what: The change in Switzerland's total economic output from the previous quarter. SECO also publishes a figure adjusted for large international sporting events, whose licensing revenues are booked in Switzerland and distort the raw number.
read: q/q is the change from the previous quarter, not annualised.
The sport-event adjusted figure gives a cleaner view of the underlying trend.
Revisions to earlier quarters can be significant.
market: Stronger growth than expected can support the franc; weaker growth can weigh on it.
Reactions are usually limited; inflation and SNB signals matter more for the franc.

name: Swiss Unemployment Rate
freq: Monthly, in the first working days of the following month, at 07:45 CET
what: The seasonally adjusted share of the labour force registered as unemployed at regional employment offices. Swiss unemployment is low by international standards and changes slowly.
read: Lower than forecast is good for the currency.
Changes of 0.1 point are already notable.
It is registered unemployment, lower than the internationally comparable ILO measure.
market: A lower rate than expected can slightly support the franc; a higher one can slightly weigh on it.
Reactions are usually small.

name: KOF Economic Barometer
source: KOF Swiss Economic Institute, ETH Zurich
freq: Monthly, on the last working day of the month at 09:00 CET
what: A composite leading indicator built from a large number of survey and economic variables. It aims to signal the direction of the Swiss economy in the near future.
read: The long-term average is 100: above means growth above average is signalled, below means below average.
The change from the previous month and the trend over several months matter.
Previous values are often revised.
market: A higher than expected reading can support the franc; a lower one can weigh on it.
Reactions are usually small.

name: Swiss Purchasing Managers' Index
freq: Monthly, on the first working days of the month, at 09:30 CET
what: A survey of purchasing managers at Swiss companies about production, orders, employment, prices and inventories. The manufacturing PMI is closely tied to export demand from Europe.
read: 50 separates expansion (above) from contraction (below).
Compare with the forecast and the previous month; Swiss PMIs can be volatile.
Weakness often follows weak euro-area demand.
market: A higher than expected reading can support the franc; a lower one can weigh on it.
Reactions are usually small and short-lived.

name: Swiss Retail Sales
freq: Monthly, about one month after the reference month, at 08:30 CET
what: The change in real retail turnover compared with the same month a year earlier, adjusted for sales days and holidays. It reflects household spending in Switzerland.
read: The y/y figure is volatile and often revised.
Calendar effects and cross-border shopping can distort single months.
market: Stronger sales than expected can slightly support the franc; weaker sales can slightly weigh on it.
Reactions are usually small.

name: UBS-CFA Economic Expectations (formerly Credit Suisse)
freq: Monthly, usually mid-month on the same day as ZEW, at 10:00 CET
what: A survey of financial analysts about their expectations for the Swiss economy over the next six months. It was run by Credit Suisse with the CFA Society until UBS took it over.
read: It is a balance of optimists minus pessimists; positive means more expect improvement.
The change from the previous month matters more than the level.
market: A higher than expected reading can slightly support the franc; reactions are usually small.

name: Consumer Price Index
freq: Monthly, usually the third Wednesday after the month ends, 07:00 UK time
what: Measures the change in prices of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by UK households. CPI is the measure the Bank of England's 2% inflation target is set on, so it feeds directly into interest-rate decisions. Core CPI excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.
read: Compare the actual figure with the forecast: the surprise drives the move, not the level alone.
Headline CPI y/y is the target measure; core y/y shows underlying, sticky inflation.
Services CPI, published in the same release, is watched closely by the MPC as a gauge of domestic price pressure.
m/m readings are seasonal (for example April, when regulated prices and bills reset); y/y is cleaner for trend.
market: Higher than expected → markets price fewer or later Bank Rate cuts → gilt yields rise → GBP tends to strengthen.
Lower than expected → more cuts priced → GBP tends to weaken; GBP/USD, EUR/GBP and GBP/JPY react first.
If inflation rises while growth is weak, the market may read it as stagflation and the pound's gain can fade.
A gap of more than 1 percentage point from target obliges the Governor to write an open letter to the Chancellor.

name: Producer Price Index and Retail Price Index
freq: Monthly, released together with CPI, 07:00 UK time
what: PPI Input measures prices UK manufacturers pay for materials and fuel; PPI Output measures the prices they charge at the factory gate. RPI is an older consumer inflation measure still used for index-linked gilts, rail fares and some wage deals.
read: Input prices can signal future pressure on output prices and, later, on consumer prices.
PPI swings with oil, commodities and sterling's exchange rate; m/m is volatile.
RPI usually runs above CPI because of its formula and housing costs; it is not the BoE target.
These usually move markets far less than CPI released at the same minute.
market: Higher producer prices → hint of more inflation ahead → slightly higher rate expectations → mildly GBP positive.
The reaction is usually swamped by the CPI print released at the same time.
RPI matters for index-linked gilt investors more than for currency traders.

name: Gross Domestic Product
freq: Monthly GDP about six weeks after the month ends; the first quarterly estimate comes with the third month of the quarter; final estimate near the end of the following quarter; 07:00 UK time
what: Measures the total value of goods and services produced in the UK, the broadest gauge of economic activity. The UK is one of few countries publishing an official monthly GDP estimate, alongside the quarterly figures.
read: Monthly GDP m/m is noisy (weather, strikes, holidays); a three-month view gives the trend.
Prelim q/q is the first quarterly estimate and moves markets most; Final q/q is a revision and usually moves less.
Two consecutive negative quarters is the common technical definition of recession.
The same release includes services, production and construction output, which show what drove growth.
market: Stronger growth → less need for rate cuts → higher gilt yields → GBP tends to strengthen.
Weak growth → more cuts priced → GBP tends to weaken, especially against EUR and USD.
If inflation is the BoE's main concern, a growth surprise can matter less than CPI and wage data.
Large revisions to earlier months can matter as much as the headline.

name: UK output, trade and investment details
freq: Mostly released with monthly GDP, 07:00 UK time; current account and business investment with the quarterly GDP releases
what: Breakdowns of UK activity: factory and industrial output, construction, services, business investment, and trade with the rest of the world. They explain what is behind the headline GDP figure.
read: Most are released at the same minute as GDP, so the GDP surprise usually dominates.
Production and construction are small, volatile parts of the economy; services is about four-fifths of output.
Trade balance is in pounds; a smaller deficit is read as positive.
Business investment shows whether firms are confident enough to spend.
market: Better-than-expected details support growth expectations → modestly GBP positive.
A strong headline with weak details (or the reverse) can make the pound's reaction fade.
A persistent current-account deficit is a long-run weak point for sterling, rarely a release-day driver.

name: Claimant Count Change
source: Office for National Statistics (ONS), from DWP benefit data
freq: Monthly, in the labour market release (usually a Tuesday mid-month), 07:00 UK time
what: The change in the number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits in the previous month. It is timelier than the survey-based unemployment rate but is affected by changes in benefit rules (Universal Credit).
read: Lower than expected (fewer new claimants) is good for the currency.
Benefit-rule changes can distort it; the ONS labels it experimental-quality.
Read together with unemployment rate and wages, published in the same release.
market: Fewer claimants → tighter labour market → more wage pressure → fewer rate cuts → GBP tends to strengthen.
Wage growth in the same release usually matters more for the Bank of England.
Large surprises can move GBP/USD and EUR/GBP at 07:00 before London opens fully.

name: Unemployment Rate (ILO, three-month average)
source: Office for National Statistics (ONS), Labour Force Survey
freq: Monthly, in the labour market release (usually a Tuesday mid-month), 07:00 UK time; covers the three months ending about six weeks earlier
what: The share of the labour force that is out of work and actively looking for a job, from the Labour Force Survey. It is a rolling three-month average, so it moves slowly.
read: Lower than expected is good for the currency.
The survey has had low response rates since 2023; the ONS warns the figures are less reliable and is rebuilding it.
A rising rate is a key sign of slack that would allow the BoE to cut rates.
market: Lower unemployment → tighter labour market → fewer rate cuts priced → GBP tends to strengthen.
Because of data-quality doubts, markets often give more weight to wages and payroll (HMRC PAYE) data.
A sharp rise can push gilt yields and GBP lower together.

name: Average Weekly Earnings (three months, year on year)
freq: Monthly, in the labour market release (usually a Tuesday mid-month), 07:00 UK time
what: Annual growth in average weekly pay, averaged over three months, with and without bonuses. Wage growth is a main driver of services inflation, which the Bank of England watches closely.
read: Higher than expected is good for the currency.
Pay excluding bonuses (regular pay) is the cleaner trend; bonuses are lumpy, especially in finance.
Private-sector regular pay is the series MPC members cite most often.
Compare with inflation: wages well above CPI keep inflation pressure alive.
market: Faster wage growth → stickier services inflation → fewer or later rate cuts → GBP tends to strengthen.
Often the most market-moving item in the labour release.
Watch gilt yields and rate-cut pricing alongside GBP/USD and EUR/GBP.

name: Retail Sales
freq: Monthly, about three to four weeks after the month ends (usually a Friday), 07:00 UK time
what: Measures the volume of goods sold by retailers in Great Britain. It is a timely gauge of household spending; core excludes automotive fuel.
read: m/m is the headline; it is volatile (weather, Black Friday timing, seasonal adjustment).
Volumes, not values, are reported, so price changes are stripped out.
Retail is a modest part of total consumer spending; services spending is not included.
Revisions to the previous month can be large.
market: Stronger spending → better growth and inflation outlook → fewer rate cuts → GBP tends to strengthen.
Weak sales → consumer stress → GBP tends to weaken.
Surprises often reverse if the prior month is revised the other way.

name: UK Purchasing Managers' Index (S&P Global UK PMI)
freq: Flash around the 23rd of the month, 09:30 UK time; final manufacturing on the first business day and services on the third business day of the next month; construction on the fourth
what: Monthly surveys of purchasing managers asking whether output, new orders, employment and prices are rising or falling. It is one of the first indicators of each month's activity.
read: 50 separates expansion (above) from contraction (below); the distance from 50 shows breadth.
Flash readings move markets most; finals are usually small revisions.
Services matters more than manufacturing for the UK economy.
The survey's input and output price components are watched as early inflation signals.
market: Better than expected → stronger growth outlook → GBP tends to strengthen.
Reactions are usually bigger at the flash release, released alongside eurozone flash PMIs.
Rising price components can lift rate expectations even when activity is weak.

name: Bank of England interest rate decision (Bank Rate)
source: Bank of England, Monetary Policy Committee
freq: Eight times a year, 12:00 UK time (usually a Thursday); the Summary and minutes are published at the same time
what: The nine-member Monetary Policy Committee sets Bank Rate, the rate the Bank pays on reserves, which anchors UK borrowing costs. The aim is to keep CPI inflation at 2%. The Monetary Policy Summary and minutes explain the decision.
read: The decision is usually expected; the vote split (for example 5–4 versus 7–2) often matters more.
Wording on the future path of rates ('gradual', 'careful') shapes expectations for the next meetings.
Compare with market pricing (OIS), not only economists' forecasts.
A dissent toward cutting or hiking signals where the committee is heading.
market: A hawkish surprise (hike, fewer cut votes, firm language) → higher gilt yields → GBP tends to strengthen.
A dovish surprise (cut, more cut votes) → GBP tends to weaken.
A cut that is fully priced can still lift GBP if the guidance is less dovish than feared.
GBP pairs, gilts and UK bank stocks react within seconds of 12:00.

name: Monetary Policy Report, press conference and Governor's remarks
freq: Report four times a year (February, May, August, November) with the rate decision; press conference about 30 minutes later; Governor's speeches and Treasury Committee hearings as scheduled
what: The Monetary Policy Report sets out the Bank's forecasts for growth, unemployment and inflation. The Governor presents it at a press conference and testifies to Parliament's Treasury Committee. Speeches by the Governor can shift expectations for Bank Rate.
read: Look at the inflation forecast two to three years ahead: above 2% signals caution on cuts.
The forecasts are conditioned on market rate expectations; the Bank's comments on that path are key.
In speeches, listen for comments on the next meeting, wage growth and services inflation.
No forecast for these events: the market reacts to tone versus expectations.
market: Hawkish tone (inflation risks, patience on cuts) → GBP tends to strengthen.
Dovish tone (weak growth, inflation falling faster) → GBP tends to weaken.
Q&A answers can move GBP more than prepared remarks.
Comments on financial stability or gilt markets can also move long-term yields.

name: MPC member speeches
freq: Irregular; listed in the Bank's speeches calendar
what: Speeches, interviews and panel appearances by members of the Monetary Policy Committee, including the deputy governors, the chief economist and the four external members. Each member votes individually, so their views hint at future vote splits.
read: Compare the speaker's tone with their recent votes: a shift is news, a repeat is not.
Members known for dissent (on either side) move markets less when they repeat their view.
Comments about the next meeting or the pace of cuts matter most.
Speeches during the quiet period before a decision do not normally take place.
market: Hawkish comments → fewer cuts priced → GBP tends to strengthen.
Dovish comments → GBP tends to weaken.
Most speeches cause small moves; impact grows when markets are split on the next decision.

name: Bank of England financial stability publications and inflation letter
source: Bank of England (Financial Policy Committee, Monetary Policy Committee)
freq: Financial Stability Report twice a year with FPC records; inflation letter only when CPI is more than 1 percentage point from 2%, published with the CPI-following decision; surveys quarterly
what: The Financial Policy Committee reviews risks to the UK financial system (banks, housing, debt, markets) and can adjust tools such as bank capital buffers. The inflation letter is an open letter from the Governor explaining why inflation is off target and what the Bank is doing.
read: Look for changes to bank capital requirements or mortgage rules.
Warnings about market stress or gilt market functioning can matter for long yields.
The inflation letter repeats the MPC's view; news comes only if it changes the expected path.
Surveys of credit conditions and inflation expectations feed the MPC's thinking.
market: Usually limited impact on GBP; bank stocks react more.
Signs of financial stress can weigh on GBP and lift demand for safe assets.
Higher household inflation expectations can raise rate expectations modestly.

name: UK Budget and fiscal statements
source: HM Treasury, with forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)
freq: Budget once a year (usually autumn) and a spring forecast statement; the Chancellor speaks around 12:30 UK time, OBR forecasts follow
what: The Chancellor sets out tax and spending plans; the independent OBR publishes growth, inflation and borrowing forecasts alongside. It shapes gilt issuance and the fiscal backdrop for the Bank of England.
read: Key items: borrowing path, headroom against fiscal rules, gilt issuance plans and tax changes.
OBR growth and inflation forecasts show how policy may affect the BoE outlook.
Measures that raise inflation (for example indirect taxes) can delay rate cuts.
There is no forecast number; reaction depends on credibility and on what was leaked beforehand.
market: Credible plans and stable borrowing → calmer gilts → supportive for GBP.
Fears about unfunded borrowing → gilt yields rise for the wrong reasons → GBP can fall with gilts, as in September 2022.
Growth-boosting or inflationary measures can raise rate expectations and support GBP.
Gilts, GBP and UK domestic stocks can all move sharply during and after the speech.

name: Public Sector Net Borrowing
freq: Monthly, around the 20th, 07:00 UK time
what: The UK government's monthly borrowing: spending minus revenue, excluding public sector banks. It tracks whether the government is on course for its fiscal plans.
read: Lower borrowing than expected is treated as good for the currency.
Monthly figures swing with tax-payment timing (January self-assessment receipts).
Compare the year-to-date total with the OBR forecast.
market: Usually little impact on GBP.
Large overshoots can push gilt yields higher on supply worries, especially before a Budget.
Matters more when markets are already worried about UK public finances.

name: GfK Consumer Confidence Index
freq: Monthly, usually the last Friday of the month (sometimes earlier), 00:01 UK time
what: A survey of about 2,000 UK adults on their personal finances, the general economy and whether now is a good time for major purchases. It is an early signal of consumer spending.
read: The index is a balance: negative means pessimists outnumber optimists; the UK reading is usually negative.
The change versus forecast and the trend matter more than the level.
Sub-indices on major purchases and personal finances are most linked to spending.
market: Better confidence → expectations of stronger spending → mildly GBP positive.
