Released overnight in thin trading, so moves are usually small.
Large drops around political or fiscal events can add to GBP weakness.

name: BRC Retail Sales Monitor and Shop Price Index
source: British Retail Consortium (BRC), with KPMG (sales) and NielsenIQ (prices)
freq: Monthly, sales usually on the second Tuesday, shop prices around the start of the month, 00:01 UK time
what: The Retail Sales Monitor reports annual growth in the value of sales at large UK retailers. The Shop Price Index measures inflation in prices of goods sold in shops, including food.
read: Sales are in value, so higher prices lift the figure even if volumes are flat.
They come before the official ONS retail sales and CPI data.
Calendar effects (Easter, Black Friday) can distort year-on-year comparisons.
market: Usually small moves, released overnight.
A big surprise can shift expectations for the ONS retail sales release.
Rising shop prices hint at food inflation pressure watched by the BoE.

name: Nationwide House Price Index
freq: Monthly, around the first business day of the month, 07:00 UK time
what: Measures changes in UK house prices based on Nationwide's own mortgage approvals. It is one of the earliest house-price readings each month.
read: m/m is the headline on the calendar; y/y gives the trend.
Based only on Nationwide's lending, so it differs from the official ONS index.
Seasonally adjusted figures are used for the monthly change.
market: Rising prices → household wealth and confidence → mildly GBP positive.
Usually small impact; it matters more when housing is under stress from high mortgage rates.
UK housebuilder stocks often react more than the pound.

name: Other UK house price indicators
freq: Monthly; Halifax around the 7th, RICS survey in the second week (00:01 UK time), ONS HPI with the CPI release
what: Halifax measures prices on its mortgage approvals. RICS surveys surveyors on whether prices are rising or falling, expressed as a net balance. The ONS HPI uses completed sales from the Land Registry and lags by about two months.
read: RICS is a balance: positive means more surveyors see rising prices.
Halifax and Nationwide can disagree month to month.
ONS HPI is the most complete but the most delayed.
market: Generally low impact on GBP.
A sharp housing slowdown can raise expectations of rate cuts → GBP weaker.
Housebuilder and bank stocks react more than the currency.

name: Money and Credit (mortgage approvals, lending, M4)
freq: Monthly, around the end of the month or first business days, 09:30 UK time
what: Bank of England data on lending to households and firms, mortgage approvals for house purchase, and broad money (M4). They show how higher or lower rates are passing through to borrowing.
read: Mortgage approvals are a leading indicator for house prices and sales.
Net lending shows how much households are borrowing after repayments.
Higher numbers point to stronger demand for credit.
market: Stronger lending → firmer housing and spending → mildly GBP positive.
Usually low impact on the currency.
A collapse in approvals can feed expectations of rate cuts.

name: CBI Industrial Trends and Distributive Trades surveys
freq: Monthly, usually in the second half of the month, 11:00 UK time
what: Surveys of UK manufacturers (order books) and retailers (sales versus a year ago), reported as net balances of firms reporting increases minus decreases.
read: A positive balance means more firms report increases than decreases; UK readings are often negative.
The change versus forecast and the trend matter more than the level.
Small samples make the retail balance volatile.
market: Better balances → mildly GBP positive.
Usually low impact; PMIs are the main business survey for markets.
Price-expectation questions can matter when inflation is the focus.

name: Bank of Japan policy decision, Outlook Report and press conference
freq: Eight two-day meetings a year; the decision has no fixed time (usually around midday Tokyo time); Governor's press conference about 15:30 Tokyo time; Outlook Report quarterly (January, April, July, October)
what: The BoJ's nine-member Policy Board sets the short-term policy rate (the uncollateralised overnight call rate) and decides on government bond purchases. The Outlook Report gives forecasts for growth and inflation against the 2% price stability target. The BoJ ended negative rates in March 2024 and has been raising rates gradually since.
read: Compare the decision with expectations and with overnight index swap pricing.
Dissenting votes and any changes to bond-purchase plans are important signals.
In the Outlook Report, core CPI forecasts at or above 2% support further hikes.
The Governor's answers at the press conference often move JPY more than the statement.
market: A hike or hawkish guidance → higher Japanese yields → narrower gap with US yields → JPY tends to strengthen.
A dovish hold or caution on hikes → JPY tends to weaken; USD/JPY and EUR/JPY react most.
A stronger yen can hurt the Nikkei and trigger unwinding of carry trades across markets.
The decision time is not fixed, so the move can come without warning during the Tokyo session.

name: BoJ Summary of Opinions, meeting minutes and BoJ core CPI
freq: Summary of Opinions about six business days after each meeting, 08:50 Tokyo time; minutes after the following meeting; BoJ core CPI measures monthly
what: The Summary of Opinions lists, without names, the views board members expressed at the latest meeting. The minutes give the full discussion with a delay. The BoJ also publishes its own underlying-inflation measures.
read: Look for how many members talk about the timing of the next hike.
Concerns about the yen's weakness and import prices are hawkish signals.
Minutes are old news by the time they appear, so they usually move markets little.
market: Hawkish opinions → expectations of earlier hikes → JPY tends to strengthen.
Dovish opinions → JPY tends to weaken.
The Summary can move USD/JPY in early Tokyo trading; minutes rarely do.

name: Bank of Japan Governor and board member speeches
freq: Irregular; the BoJ publishes a schedule of speeches and press conferences
what: Speeches, parliamentary testimony and interviews by the Governor, deputy governors and Policy Board members. Because the BoJ moves cautiously and signals in advance, these remarks are a main source of guidance on the next move.
read: The Governor carries the most weight; listen for hints about the next meeting.
Comments about wage negotiations (shunto), inflation and the weak yen are key signals.
Board members' regional speeches often include a press conference with clearer answers.
market: Hawkish remarks → higher expected Japanese rates → JPY tends to strengthen.
Dovish remarks → JPY tends to weaken; USD/JPY and cross-yen pairs react.
Comments on the currency itself can move JPY more than comments on rates.

name: Consumer Price Index (National and Tokyo)
source: Statistics Bureau, Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC)
freq: Tokyo CPI for the current month on the last Friday of the month; National CPI for the previous month around the third Friday; 08:30 Tokyo time
what: Measures changes in the prices of goods and services bought by households. In Japan, 'core' CPI excludes fresh food (not energy). Tokyo CPI comes out about three weeks before the national figure and is used as an early signal.
read: Core CPI y/y (ex fresh food) is the main measure; the BoJ's target is 2%.
The 'core-core' measure (ex fresh food and energy) shows underlying inflation.
Government energy subsidies and changes to fees (such as school fees) can distort the figures.
Tokyo CPI is used to anticipate the national number.
market: Higher inflation → more expected BoJ hikes → JPY tends to strengthen.
Lower inflation → hikes delayed → JPY tends to weaken.
Moves are usually moderate; inflation matters most just before a BoJ meeting.
USD/JPY's direction is also driven heavily by US yields.

name: Corporate Goods Price Index and Services Producer Price Index
freq: Monthly; CGPI (PPI) around the 10th, SPPI around the 25th, 08:50 Tokyo time
what: The Corporate Goods Price Index measures prices of goods traded between companies; the Services PPI measures prices of services between companies. They show cost pressures that can pass through to consumer prices.
read: Import prices and the yen's exchange rate strongly affect goods prices.
Services producer prices give a view of domestic, wage-driven inflation.
Usually second-tier: moves are small compared with CPI.
market: Higher producer prices → signs of persistent inflation → mildly JPY positive.
Usually little impact on USD/JPY.

name: Gross Domestic Product
source: Economic and Social Research Institute, Cabinet Office
freq: Quarterly; preliminary about six to seven weeks after the quarter ends, revised (final) about a month later; 08:50 Tokyo time
what: Measures the total value of goods and services produced in Japan. The price index (GDP deflator) shows domestic inflation across the whole economy.
read: q/q is the headline; Japan also reports an annualised rate (about four times q/q).
Revisions between preliminary and final estimates can be large, often from business investment.
Private consumption and capital spending show domestic demand; net exports can swing the headline.
market: Stronger growth → more room for BoJ hikes → JPY tends to strengthen.
Weak growth → BoJ caution → JPY tends to weaken.
The Nikkei can react positively to strong data even as a firmer yen weighs on exporters.

name: Tankan Survey (Short-Term Economic Survey of Enterprises)
freq: Quarterly, early April, July and October and mid-December, 08:50 Tokyo time
what: The BoJ's survey of around 9,000 Japanese companies on business conditions, prices, employment and investment plans. It is one of the main inputs into the BoJ's policy decisions.
read: Indices are diffusion indices: share of firms saying conditions are good minus share saying bad; zero is neutral.
The large manufacturers index is the headline; large non-manufacturers reflect domestic services.
Capex plans and firms' inflation expectations are watched by the BoJ.
Compare with the forecast and the previous quarter.
market: Better business conditions → stronger case for BoJ hikes → JPY tends to strengthen.
Weaker readings → JPY tends to weaken.
Released before a BoJ meeting, it can shape expectations for that meeting.

name: Japan Purchasing Managers' Index (S&P Global Japan PMI)
source: S&P Global (previously sponsored as au Jibun Bank Japan PMI)
freq: Flash around the 23rd of the month, 09:30 Tokyo time; finals in the first business days of the following month
what: Monthly surveys of purchasing managers at Japanese manufacturers and service firms on output, orders, jobs and prices. It gives an early read on activity.
read: 50 separates expansion from contraction.
Flash readings matter most; finals are usually small revisions.
Price components are watched as signals of inflation pressure.
market: Better readings → mildly JPY positive.
Usually small impact; the yen is driven more by the BoJ and US yields.
Stronger readings can support the Nikkei and broader risk appetite in Asia.

name: Average Cash Earnings (Monthly Labour Survey)
source: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW)
freq: Monthly, early in the month for two months earlier, 08:30 Tokyo time
what: Annual growth in average total cash earnings per worker. The BoJ wants wage growth that supports sustained 2% inflation, so this is one of its key data points.
read: Higher wage growth is good for the currency.
Bonus months (June–August, December) make the headline volatile; scheduled earnings are steadier.
Real wages (adjusted for inflation) show whether households can sustain spending.
Sample changes can distort comparisons; preliminary figures are revised.
market: Faster wage growth → stronger case for BoJ hikes → JPY tends to strengthen.
Weak wages → BoJ caution → JPY tends to weaken.
Matters more around spring wage negotiations (shunto) and before BoJ meetings.

name: Unemployment Rate and jobs-to-applicants ratio
source: Statistics Bureau (MIC) for unemployment; Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare for the jobs ratio
freq: Monthly, around the end of the month, 08:30 Tokyo time
what: The share of the labour force without work and seeking a job, from the Labour Force Survey. The jobs-to-applicants ratio shows how many job openings there are per job seeker.
read: Lower unemployment is good for the currency.
Japan's unemployment is structurally low and moves in small steps (0.1 points).
A jobs ratio above 1 means more openings than applicants.
market: Usually small impact on JPY.
A tight labour market supports wage growth and the case for BoJ hikes.

name: Household Spending and Retail Sales
source: Statistics Bureau (MIC) for household spending; Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) for retail sales
freq: Monthly; household spending early in the month, 08:30 Tokyo time; retail sales around the end of the month, 08:50 Tokyo time
what: Household Spending measures real spending by households of two or more people from a survey. Retail Sales measures the value of sales at retailers. Together they show the strength of consumer demand.
read: Household Spending is real (inflation-adjusted) and volatile because of its small sample.
Retail Sales is in value terms, so inflation lifts it.
Look at trends over several months rather than one reading.
market: Stronger consumption → support for BoJ hikes → mildly JPY positive.
Usually small impact on USD/JPY.

name: Industrial Production, Machinery Orders and Tertiary Industry Activity
source: METI (industrial production, tertiary industry); Cabinet Office (machinery orders)
freq: Monthly; preliminary industrial production around the end of the month, 08:50 Tokyo time; revised about two weeks later
what: Industrial Production measures output from Japan's factories, mines and utilities. Core Machinery Orders (excluding ships and electric power) is a leading indicator of business investment. Tertiary Industry Activity covers services.
read: Preliminary figures matter more than revised ones.
Production is volatile; car output and supply-chain disruptions swing it.
Machinery orders are very volatile month to month.
market: Better data → mildly JPY positive.
Usually low impact; more relevant for the Nikkei and Japanese exporters.

name: Trade Balance and Current Account
source: Ministry of Finance (trade, from customs data; current account with the BoJ)
freq: Trade balance monthly around the third week, 08:50 Tokyo time; current account monthly, about five to six weeks after the month
what: The trade balance is exports minus imports of goods. The current account adds income from investments abroad, which is large for Japan. Exporters and investors converting foreign earnings create demand for yen.
read: A larger surplus (or smaller deficit) is treated as good for the yen.
Energy import costs swing Japan's trade balance.
Export growth y/y is a gauge of global demand, especially from China and the US.
market: Larger surplus → more structural demand for yen → mildly JPY positive.
Usually small release-day moves.
Over months, persistent deficits from energy imports have been one source of yen weakness.

name: Economy Watchers Survey, Consumer Confidence and Leading Indicators
freq: Monthly; Economy Watchers around the 8th, 14:00 Tokyo time; Consumer Confidence near the end of the month; Leading Indicators about five weeks after the month
what: The Economy Watchers survey asks workers in close contact with consumers and businesses (shop staff, taxi drivers) about current conditions. Consumer Confidence surveys households. The Leading Index combines indicators that tend to turn before the economy.
read: Economy Watchers and Consumer Confidence: 50 is neutral.
Leading Indicators are a composite index level; direction matters more than level.
These are second-tier; trends over several months matter more than one reading.
market: Better sentiment → mildly JPY positive.
Usually very small impact.

name: Money, lending and JGB auctions
source: Bank of Japan (money and lending); Ministry of Finance (JGB auctions)
freq: Money and lending monthly, 08:50 Tokyo time; JGB auctions on a set monthly schedule, results around 12:35 Tokyo time
what: Bank Lending and M2 track credit and money growth. JGB auctions show demand for Japanese government bonds; weak demand at long maturities has become a market focus as the BoJ reduces its purchases.
read: For auctions, the result shows the yield accepted and the bid-to-cover ratio (demand relative to amount sold).
A low bid-to-cover or a wide tail signals weak demand.
Money and lending growth are slow-moving and rarely surprise.
market: Weak long-bond auctions → higher JGB yields → can lift JPY, or weaken it if seen as fiscal stress.
Money and lending data usually do not move JPY.

name: Official NBS Purchasing Managers' Index
source: National Bureau of Statistics of China (NBS) with the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing
freq: Monthly, on the last day of the month, 09:30 Beijing time
what: The official survey of purchasing managers at about 3,200 manufacturers and at non-manufacturing firms (services and construction). It covers more large and state-owned companies than the private RatingDog survey.
read: 50 separates expansion from contraction.
New export orders show external demand; the price sub-indices show deflation or inflation pressure.
Lunar New Year makes January–February readings hard to compare.
Compare with forecast and with the RatingDog PMI released the next day.
market: Better readings → stronger outlook for China → supports CNY and especially AUD and NZD.
Also moves industrial metals, iron ore and Asian stock markets.
CNY is managed by the PBoC (daily fixing), so the reaction often shows more in AUD/USD than USD/CNY.

name: RatingDog China General Manufacturing and Services PMI (formerly Caixin)
source: S&P Global, sponsored by RatingDog (Caixin until mid-2025)
freq: Monthly; manufacturing on the first business day, services on the third business day, 09:45 Beijing time
what: A private survey of purchasing managers compiled by S&P Global. Compared with the official NBS PMI, it has more weight on smaller, private and export-oriented companies. The sponsor changed from Caixin to RatingDog in 2025; the survey method stayed the same.
read: 50 separates expansion from contraction.
It can diverge from the NBS PMI because the samples differ.
New export orders and employment are the key details.
market: Better readings → supportive for CNY and China-linked currencies such as AUD and NZD.
Also affects metals, iron ore and Asian equities.
Impact is often larger when it confirms or contradicts the official PMI from the day before.

name: Gross Domestic Product
source: National Bureau of Statistics of China (NBS)
freq: Quarterly, around mid-month after the quarter ends (mid-January, April, July, October), 10:00 Beijing time
what: Measures China's total economic output. The government sets an annual growth target (around 5% in recent years), so GDP is judged against that target as well as the forecast.
read: y/y is the headline in China; q/q is seasonally adjusted and secondary.
Results rarely stray far from the official target; small misses can still matter.
Released together with monthly industrial production, retail sales and investment data.
The GDP deflator (nominal vs real growth) shows deflation pressure.
market: Stronger growth → supports CNY, AUD, NZD and commodities.
Weak growth raises expectations of stimulus, which can lift Chinese stocks even as the data disappoint.
The CNY reaction is limited by the PBoC's management of the exchange rate.

name: Monthly activity data (industrial production, retail sales, fixed-asset investment, unemployment)
source: National Bureau of Statistics of China (NBS)
freq: Monthly, around the 15th–17th, 10:00 Beijing time, followed by an NBS press conference; January and February are combined
what: Industrial Production measures output of larger industrial firms. Retail Sales measures consumer goods sales. Fixed Asset Investment shows spending on infrastructure, property and manufacturing, year to date. The surveyed urban unemployment rate is also published.
read: All are year-on-year; fixed-asset investment is cumulative year to date.
Retail sales show the strength of domestic consumption, a key policy focus.
Property investment within fixed-asset investment shows the state of the housing slump.
Lower unemployment is better; youth unemployment is published separately.
market: Better data → supports CNY, AUD, NZD and industrial metals.
Weak data can lift expectations of stimulus and PBoC easing.
Moves are often clearer in AUD/USD and copper than in USD/CNY.

name: Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index
source: National Bureau of Statistics of China (NBS)
freq: Monthly, around the 9th–10th, 09:30 Beijing time
what: CPI measures prices paid by consumers; PPI measures factory-gate prices. China has seen very low consumer inflation and falling producer prices in recent years, so these are read as gauges of deflation and weak demand.
read: Pork prices strongly affect China's CPI; core CPI (ex food and energy) shows underlying demand.
Negative PPI means factory-gate deflation, which China also exports to the world.
Lunar New Year timing distorts January and February readings.
market: Higher readings → signs of recovering demand → supportive for CNY and China-linked assets.
Low or negative readings → expectations of PBoC easing and stimulus.
Rate reasoning differs from other countries: higher inflation here is read mainly as stronger demand.

name: Trade Balance (exports and imports)
source: General Administration of Customs of China
freq: Monthly, usually around the 7th–10th, no fixed time (often late morning Beijing time); January and February are often combined
what: Exports minus imports of goods, published in yuan and in US dollars. Exports show global demand for Chinese goods; imports show domestic demand and China's appetite for commodities.
read: A larger surplus is treated as good for CNY.
Look at exports and imports y/y separately: a surplus from falling imports signals weak domestic demand.
Imports of iron ore, copper, oil and soybeans are watched by commodity markets.
Tariffs and trade disputes can shift exports to and from the US sharply.
market: Strong exports and imports → supportive for CNY, AUD and commodities.
Weak imports can hurt AUD and commodity prices even if the surplus is large.
Exports to the US matter for trade-tension headlines.

name: New Yuan Loans, M2 and Total Social Financing
freq: Monthly, usually between the 10th and 15th, no fixed time
what: New Loans measures new yuan lending by banks during the month. Total Social Financing is a broader measure of credit including bonds. M2 is broad money. They show whether credit is flowing to households and firms.
read: Lending is seasonal: very large in January, weaker in months like July and October.
The split between household and corporate loans shows demand; weak household loans signal a soft housing market.
Compare with the same month of previous years.
market: Stronger credit growth → stronger economy ahead → supportive for CNY, AUD and metals.
Weak credit can raise expectations of PBoC easing.
Release time is irregular, so the reaction can come unexpectedly.

name: Loan Prime Rate (1-year and 5-year)
source: People's Bank of China, via the National Interbank Funding Center
freq: Monthly, on the 20th (next business day if a holiday), 09:00 Beijing time
what: The benchmark lending rates quoted by a panel of banks, used to price most new loans in China. The 1-year LPR is used for most corporate and household loans; the 5-year LPR is the reference for mortgages. The LPR follows the PBoC's main policy rate, the 7-day reverse repo rate.
read: Higher than expected (or a smaller cut) is treated as good for the currency.
LPR changes usually follow a cut in the 7-day reverse repo rate announced earlier.
A bigger cut in the 5-year LPR targets the property market.
market: A cut → lower Chinese yields → wider gap with US yields → CNY tends to weaken.
Cuts can still lift Chinese stocks and AUD if seen as supporting growth.
Unchanged rates in line with expectations usually cause little reaction.

name: People's Bank of China Governor speeches
freq: Irregular; often at forums such as the Lujiazui Forum, press conferences of the State Council Information Office, or the National People's Congress
what: Public remarks by the PBoC Governor and officials. The PBoC sets policy rates, banks' reserve requirement ratio and the daily yuan fixing, so comments can signal easing or measures to support the currency.
read: Hints of cuts to rates or the reserve requirement ratio (RRR) are the main signal.
Comments about keeping the yuan 'basically stable' signal defence of the exchange rate.
Large stimulus packages are sometimes announced at joint press conferences.
market: Easing signals → CNY tends to weaken, while Chinese stocks and AUD may rise on growth hopes.
Signals of currency support → CNY steadier or stronger.
The yuan's daily fixing often reacts more than spot moves.

name: Other Chinese indicators (FDI, industrial profits, new home prices)
source: Ministry of Commerce (FDI); NBS (industrial profits, home prices); The Conference Board (leading index)
freq: Monthly; industrial profits around the 27th, 09:30 Beijing time; home prices with the mid-month activity data
what: Foreign Direct Investment shows money invested in China by foreign companies. Industrial Profits shows profits of larger industrial firms. New Home Prices track prices in 70 major cities and the state of the property market.
read: Positive changes are good for the currency.
Home prices show whether the property slump is easing.
These are second-tier and usually move markets only on big surprises.
market: Better data → mildly supportive for CNY and China-linked assets.
Property data can move Chinese developers' stocks and iron ore more than currencies.

name: RBA Cash Rate Decision and Statement
freq: 8 times a year; decision and statement at 2:30 pm Sydney time on the second day of the meeting
what: The Monetary Policy Board of the Reserve Bank of Australia sets the target for the overnight cash rate, the main policy rate in Australia. The statement released with the decision explains the Board's view on inflation, jobs and the outlook. The RBA's goals are inflation of 2–3% and full employment.
read: The decision is usually expected; markets price the outcome in advance from rate futures.
A surprise change versus forecast causes the largest moves.
When the rate is unchanged, the statement's wording on future moves matters most.
Watch changes in phrases about inflation risks and whether the Board sees further moves as likely.
market: Higher rate or hawkish tone → higher Australian yields → AUD tends to strengthen.
Cut or dovish tone → AUD tends to weaken.
AUD/USD, AUD/JPY, AUD/NZD and ASX 200 futures react first.
A widely expected hike can still weaken AUD if the statement signals it is the last one.

name: RBA Governor's Press Conference
freq: After each policy decision, at 3:30 pm Sydney time
what: Since 2024 the RBA Governor holds a press conference one hour after every policy decision. The Governor explains the decision and answers journalists' questions about the outlook and the Board's thinking.
read: There is no actual/forecast number; the content is qualitative.
Listen for hints on the next move and how open the Board is to changing rates.
Comments on inflation persistence, the labour market and global risks are watched most.
Unscripted answers can differ in tone from the written statement.
market: Hawkish remarks → higher expected rates → AUD tends to rise; dovish remarks → AUD tends to fall.
Moves can extend or reverse the reaction to the decision an hour earlier.
AUD/USD and Australian bond futures react most.

name: Statement on Monetary Policy
freq: Quarterly (February, May, August, November), released with the policy decision at 2:30 pm Sydney time
what: The Statement on Monetary Policy is the RBA's quarterly report on economic conditions and its forecasts for inflation, GDP growth and unemployment. The forecasts are based on a market path for the cash rate, so they show whether the RBA sees that path as consistent with its goals.
read: Compare the new inflation forecasts with the previous Statement.
Inflation forecasts above the target band imply rates may need to be higher than markets expect.
Look at the assumed cash rate path and the RBA's discussion of risks.
Since 2024 it is published at the same time as the decision, so reactions are combined.
market: Higher inflation forecasts → higher rate expectations → AUD tends to strengthen.
Weaker growth or lower inflation forecasts → AUD tends to weaken.
AUD crosses and Australian 2-year yields react most.

name: RBA Monetary Policy Meeting Minutes
freq: Two weeks after each policy meeting, at 11:30 am Sydney time
what: The minutes summarise the Monetary Policy Board's discussion at its last meeting: the data it looked at, the options it considered and the arguments for its decision. They give more detail than the short statement on decision day.
read: No numeric forecast; the market reads the tone.
Look for which options were considered (for example a hike versus a hold).
Language on what would trigger the next move is the most important part.
Already-known decisions limit the reaction unless the minutes change the view of the next meeting.
market: More hawkish than the statement → AUD tends to rise.
More dovish than expected → AUD tends to fall.
Reaction is usually smaller than on decision day.

name: RBA Officials' Speeches
freq: Irregular; schedule published on the RBA website
what: The RBA Governor, Deputy Governor and Assistant Governors speak at conferences, parliamentary hearings and events. These remarks can update the market's view of the RBA's next policy move between meetings.
read: Speeches by the Governor carry the most weight, followed by the Deputy Governor.
Look for new views on inflation, the labour market or the timing of rate changes.
Parliamentary testimony (Senate Estimates, House committee) includes questions and can be more revealing.
Many speeches are on technical topics and cause little reaction.
market: Hawkish comments → AUD tends to rise; dovish comments → AUD tends to fall.
Impact is larger when markets are unsure about the next decision.
AUD/USD and Australian short-term yields react most.

name: Labour Force Survey: Employment Change and Unemployment Rate
freq: Monthly, usually the second or third Thursday after the month ends, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: The Labour Force Survey measures how many people are employed and how many are looking for work. Employment Change is the monthly change in the number of employed people; the Unemployment Rate is the share of the labour force without a job and looking for one. Full employment is one of the RBA's two goals.
read: Both are released together; markets weigh the unemployment rate heavily because the RBA focuses on it.
Look at full-time versus part-time jobs: full-time gains signal stronger demand.
Employment Change is volatile month to month; trend matters more than one reading.
Also check the participation rate: a falling rate can lower unemployment without more jobs.
market: More jobs or lower unemployment → higher rate expectations → AUD tends to strengthen.
Weak jobs or rising unemployment → AUD tends to weaken.
AUD/USD, AUD/NZD and Australian 3-year yields react strongly.
Large employment change with rising unemployment gives a mixed signal and a choppy reaction.

name: Consumer Price Index
freq: Monthly, at the end of the following month, 11:30 am Sydney time (complete monthly CPI since late 2025; quarterly figures before that)
what: The CPI measures the change in prices paid by households for a basket of goods and services. Since November 2025 the ABS publishes a complete monthly CPI, which replaced the quarterly CPI as the main inflation measure. Trimmed mean removes the largest price rises and falls each period and is the RBA's preferred underlying measure.
read: Trimmed mean (underlying) inflation matters more to the RBA than headline CPI.
Compare the y/y rates with the RBA's 2–3% target band.
Headline can be distorted by energy rebates, fuel and travel prices.
Older quarterly series (CPI q/q, Trimmed Mean CPI q/q) were the key releases before the monthly switch.
market: Higher inflation → higher rate expectations → AUD tends to strengthen.
Lower inflation → expectations of cuts or fewer hikes → AUD tends to weaken.
AUD/USD, AUD/NZD and Australian 3-year yields react most.
A hot headline with soft trimmed mean often produces a smaller or reversed move.

name: Wage Price Index
freq: Quarterly, about 6–7 weeks after the quarter ends, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: The Wage Price Index measures changes in the price of labour, the hourly rates paid for the same jobs, excluding bonuses and changes in hours or job mix. It shows underlying wage pressure, which the RBA watches as a driver of services inflation.
read: Higher than forecast points to stronger wage pressure.
The quarterly change is usually small; y/y gives the clearer trend.
Annual award wage decisions (effective July) lift the September quarter reading.
Compare with productivity: wages rising faster than productivity add to inflation.
market: Faster wage growth → higher inflation risk → higher rate expectations → AUD tends to rise.
Softer wages → AUD tends to weaken.
AUD/USD and Australian short-term yields react.

name: Gross Domestic Product
freq: Quarterly, about 9 weeks after the quarter ends (early March, June, September, December), 11:30 am Sydney time
what: GDP measures the total value of goods and services produced in Australia. The ABS release (National Accounts) also includes household consumption, the saving ratio and productivity, which the RBA follows closely.
read: Quarter-on-quarter growth versus forecast is the headline number.
Much of GDP is partly known from earlier data (capex, trade, construction), so surprises are often smaller.
Check household consumption and per-capita GDP, since population growth can hide weakness.
Revisions to previous quarters can change the picture.
market: Stronger growth → higher rate expectations → AUD tends to strengthen.
Weaker growth → AUD tends to weaken.
Reaction is often moderate because inflation and jobs data drive RBA decisions more.

name: Monthly Household Spending Indicator (formerly Retail Trade)
freq: Monthly, about 5–6 weeks after the month ends, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: The Monthly Household Spending Indicator measures household spending on goods and services, mainly from de-identified bank transaction data. It replaced the ABS Retail Trade publication, which ended in July 2025 (the old 'Retail Sales m/m' event). It covers services as well as goods, so it is broader than retail sales.
read: A higher than expected monthly change signals stronger consumer demand.
Look at the split between goods and services spending.
Spending figures are in current prices, so high inflation alone lifts the number.
Previous months can be revised.
market: Stronger spending → more demand pressure → higher rate expectations → AUD tends to rise.
Weak spending → AUD tends to weaken.
AUD/USD and AUD/NZD react; moves are usually smaller than for CPI or jobs.

name: International Trade in Goods (Trade Balance)
freq: Monthly, about 5 weeks after the month ends, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: The trade balance is the value of exports minus imports of goods (and services in the broader release). Australia usually runs a surplus thanks to exports of iron ore, coal, LNG and other commodities, so the balance moves strongly with commodity prices.
read: Positive means a surplus; a larger surplus than forecast is read as better.
Changes are often driven by commodity prices rather than volumes.
Check exports to China, Australia's largest market.
The market impact is usually limited.
market: Larger surplus → more foreign demand for AUD → mildly supportive.
Shrinking surplus, often from falling commodity prices → AUD tends to soften.
Iron ore and coal prices often matter more to AUD than the release itself.

name: Private New Capital Expenditure
freq: Quarterly, about 8 weeks after the quarter ends, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: This survey measures business investment in buildings, structures, equipment and machinery. It also includes firms' expected spending plans for the year ahead, which show business confidence in investment.
read: Higher than forecast quarterly growth is positive for GDP.
The spending plans (estimates) for the financial year are watched as a forward signal.
Mining and non-mining investment can move in different directions.
Feeds directly into the GDP release a week later.
market: Stronger investment → stronger growth outlook → AUD tends to rise.
Weak capex → AUD tends to fall.
Reaction is usually modest.

name: Building Approvals
freq: Monthly, about 4–5 weeks after the month ends, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: Building Approvals counts the number of dwellings approved for construction. It is a leading indicator of housing construction and of spending linked to new homes.
read: Very volatile because apartment approvals swing in large blocks.
Private house approvals give a steadier trend.
A higher than forecast change is read as positive.
Interest rates strongly influence approvals with a lag.
market: Stronger approvals → stronger housing activity → mildly supportive for AUD.
Weak approvals → mildly negative.
Market reaction is usually small.

name: Construction Work Done
freq: Quarterly, about 8 weeks after the quarter ends, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: This measures the value of building and engineering construction work done in the quarter. It feeds into GDP investment components.
read: Higher than forecast is positive for GDP.
Engineering work (mining, infrastructure) can be lumpy.
Mainly used to fine-tune GDP forecasts.
market: Stronger construction → stronger GDP expectations → mildly supportive for AUD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Private Sector Credit
freq: Monthly, at the end of the following month, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: Private Sector Credit measures the growth in lending to households and businesses by financial institutions. It shows how much borrowing, mainly for housing, is supporting spending.
read: Faster credit growth signals stronger demand and housing activity.
Housing credit is the largest component.
Movements are gradual; surprises are usually small.
market: Stronger credit → more demand → mildly supportive for AUD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Producer Price Index
freq: Quarterly, about 4 weeks after the quarter ends, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: The PPI measures changes in prices received by producers for goods and services. It is an early indicator of cost pressures that may pass through to consumer prices.
read: Higher than forecast points to stronger pipeline inflation.
Final-stage prices are most relevant for consumer inflation.
Usually less important than CPI.
market: Higher producer inflation → higher rate expectations → mildly supportive for AUD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: International Trade Price Indexes
freq: Quarterly, about 4 weeks after the quarter ends, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: These indexes measure changes in prices of imported and exported goods. Import prices feed into consumer inflation; export prices reflect commodity prices and Australia's terms of trade.
read: Higher import prices point to more imported inflation.
Export prices mostly follow commodity prices.
Usually low market impact.
market: Higher import prices → higher inflation outlook → mildly supportive for AUD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Balance of Payments: Current Account
freq: Quarterly, about 9 weeks after the quarter ends, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: The current account records trade in goods and services plus income flows with the rest of the world. It also gives the net exports contribution used for GDP the next day.
read: Value is in AUD; a larger surplus or smaller deficit than forecast is read as better.
The net exports contribution to GDP is often the most watched detail.
Mainly driven by commodity export prices.
market: Better balance → mildly supportive for AUD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index
freq: Monthly, usually on the second Tuesday, 10:30 am Sydney time
what: A survey of about 1,200 Australians on their personal finances, the economy and whether it is a good time to buy major items. It is an early signal of household spending.
read: Index above 100 means optimists outnumber pessimists; below 100 the reverse.
The monthly percentage change is the headline on ForexFactory.
No consensus forecast is usually published, so the change itself matters.
Rate decisions and inflation news shift sentiment quickly.
market: Rising sentiment → stronger spending outlook → mildly supportive for AUD.
Falling sentiment → mildly negative.
Reaction is usually small.

name: NAB Monthly Business Survey
freq: Monthly, usually the second Tuesday, 11:30 am Sydney time
what: NAB surveys several hundred businesses each month. Confidence measures expectations for the coming months; conditions combine current trading, profitability and employment. The survey also covers costs and selling prices, which hint at inflation.
read: Results are net balances: above zero means more firms report improvement than deterioration.
Business conditions reflect actual activity; confidence reflects expectations.
Price and labour cost readings are watched for inflation signals.
No widely used forecast; compare with the previous month.
market: Stronger confidence or conditions → stronger growth outlook → mildly supportive for AUD.
Weak readings → mildly negative.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Melbourne Institute Consumer Inflation Expectations
freq: Monthly, usually the second Thursday, 11:00 am Sydney time
what: A survey of consumers' expectations for inflation over the next 12 months. Central banks watch inflation expectations because they can influence wage demands and price setting.
read: Higher expectations signal a risk that inflation stays high.
Consumer expectations are often well above actual inflation; the change matters more than the level.
Usually released shortly before the jobs data in the same week.
market: Higher expectations → higher rate expectations → mildly supportive for AUD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: S&P Global Australia PMI
freq: Monthly; flash about 10 days before the month ends, final at the start of the next month
what: Purchasing Managers' Indexes survey businesses about output, new orders, employment and prices. The flash estimates are an early read of activity in the current month. Services dominate the Australian economy.
read: Above 50 means expansion; below 50 means contraction.
Flash readings move markets more than final readings.
Services PMI is more relevant for Australia than manufacturing.
Price sub-indexes hint at inflation pressure.
market: Higher PMI → stronger growth outlook → AUD tends to rise.
Lower PMI → AUD tends to weaken.
Reaction is usually modest.

name: RBNZ Official Cash Rate Decision
freq: 7 times a year at 2:00 pm New Zealand time; 4 of them come with a full Monetary Policy Statement
what: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's Monetary Policy Committee sets the Official Cash Rate (OCR), New Zealand's main policy rate. The RBNZ aims to keep annual CPI inflation between 1% and 3% over the medium term, with a focus on the 2% midpoint. Each decision comes with a Monetary Policy Review or, quarterly, a full Monetary Policy Statement with forecasts.
read: Rate decision versus forecast is the headline; markets usually price it in advance.
At Statement meetings, the projected OCR path shows where the RBNZ expects rates to go.
Changes in the projected path often move NZD more than the decision itself.
Look at the Committee's views on inflation and the risk balance.
market: Higher OCR or higher projected path → NZD tends to strengthen.
Cut or lower path → NZD tends to weaken.
NZD/USD, AUD/NZD and NZ swap rates react strongly.
A hike or cut with a signal that it is the last one can move NZD the opposite way.

name: RBNZ Press Conference
freq: After Monetary Policy Statement decisions, at 3:00 pm New Zealand time
what: After each Monetary Policy Statement the Governor and senior officials hold a press conference to explain the decision and forecasts and answer questions.
read: No number; markets read the tone.
Look for hints about the next decision and the projected OCR path.
Comments on inflation, the housing market and the economy are watched.
market: Hawkish tone → NZD tends to rise; dovish tone → NZD tends to fall.
Can extend or reverse the reaction to the decision.
NZD/USD and AUD/NZD react most.

name: RBNZ Financial Stability Report
freq: Twice a year (May and November)
what: The report assesses risks to New Zealand's financial system, including banks, housing debt and global risks. It can include comments relevant to interest rates and lending rules.
read: No number; markets react only to new policy signals.
Look for changes to lending rules (such as loan-to-value or debt-to-income limits).
Comments by the Governor at the release can matter more than the report.
market: Usually small impact on NZD unless it contains signals about monetary policy.
Tighter lending rules can lower housing activity expectations.

name: RBNZ Officials' Speeches
freq: Irregular
what: The RBNZ Governor, Deputy Governors and Chief Economist speak at events and appear before Parliament's Finance and Expenditure Committee. Their remarks can shift expectations for the Official Cash Rate between decisions.
read: The Governor's remarks carry the most weight.
Look for new views on inflation or the path of the OCR.
Parliamentary committee appearances follow Monetary Policy Statements.
market: Hawkish remarks → NZD tends to rise; dovish → NZD tends to fall.
Impact is larger when the next decision is uncertain.

name: Consumers Price Index
freq: Quarterly, about 2–3 weeks after the quarter ends, 10:45 am New Zealand time
what: The CPI measures changes in prices paid by households for goods and services. It is the RBNZ's inflation target measure (1–3% over the medium term, focusing on 2%). Because it is only quarterly, each release carries a lot of weight.
read: Compare both q/q and y/y with forecasts and with the 1–3% target band.
Non-tradable (domestic) inflation shows home-grown price pressure the RBNZ can influence.
Tradable inflation follows import prices and the exchange rate.
The RBNZ's own core measures (sectoral factor model) are watched after the release.
market: Higher inflation → higher OCR expectations → NZD tends to strengthen.
Lower inflation → NZD tends to weaken.
NZD/USD, AUD/NZD and NZ 2-year swap rates react most.

name: Selected Price Indexes
freq: Monthly, about 2–3 weeks after the month ends, 10:45 am New Zealand time
what: A monthly release covering food, rent, fuel, airfares and other prices that make up a large part of the CPI. It gives an early read of quarterly CPI before the official release.
read: Higher than forecast price growth points to a firmer quarterly CPI.
Food, fuel and rents are the main components.
Seasonal items like airfares and accommodation can swing month to month.
market: Higher prices → higher inflation expectations → mildly supportive for NZD.
Reaction is usually modest.

name: Household Labour Force Survey and Labour Cost Index
freq: Quarterly, about 5 weeks after the quarter ends, 10:45 am New Zealand time
what: The Household Labour Force Survey measures employment and unemployment in New Zealand; it is released together with wage measures, including the Labour Cost Index. Maximum sustainable employment is part of the RBNZ's remit, and wages affect domestic inflation.
read: Unemployment rate versus forecast is usually the main number.
Employment change q/q shows job growth; participation can change the unemployment rate.
Labour Cost Index shows wage pressure linked to inflation.
Quarterly releases are significant because there is no monthly equivalent.
market: Lower unemployment or stronger jobs → higher OCR expectations → NZD tends to rise.
Rising unemployment → NZD tends to fall.
NZD/USD and AUD/NZD react strongly.

name: Gross Domestic Product
freq: Quarterly, about 11 weeks after the quarter ends, 10:45 am New Zealand time
what: GDP measures the total output of the New Zealand economy. It is published later than in many countries, so other data has often already shown the trend.
read: Quarterly growth versus forecast is the headline.
A gap between Stats NZ and RBNZ forecasts can change OCR expectations.
Revisions to earlier quarters can be large.
market: Stronger growth → higher OCR expectations → NZD tends to rise.
Weak growth → NZD tends to fall.
NZD/USD and AUD/NZD react.

name: Retail Trade Survey
freq: Quarterly, about 7 weeks after the quarter ends, 10:45 am New Zealand time
what: This survey measures the volume of retail sales in New Zealand. Core retail sales exclude fuel and vehicle-related industries, which are volatile.
read: Volume changes (adjusted for prices) are reported.
Core retail sales often matter more as a trend signal.
A higher than forecast change is read as positive.
market: Stronger spending → stronger growth and inflation outlook → NZD tends to rise.
Weak sales → NZD tends to fall.

name: Overseas Merchandise Trade
freq: Monthly, about 3–4 weeks after the month ends, 10:45 am New Zealand time
what: The trade balance is the value of goods exported minus goods imported. New Zealand's exports are dominated by dairy, meat, wood and other primary products, so the balance follows commodity prices and demand from China and Australia.
read: Reported in NZD; the monthly figure and the annual total are both published.
Seasonal patterns are strong (dairy exports peak in some months).
Impact is usually limited.
market: Larger surplus or smaller deficit → mildly supportive for NZD.
Weak exports → mildly negative.
Dairy prices often matter more than the release.

name: Balance of Payments: Current Account
freq: Quarterly, about 10–11 weeks after the quarter ends, 10:45 am New Zealand time
what: The current account records trade in goods and services and income flows between New Zealand and the rest of the world. New Zealand normally runs a deficit, funded by foreign capital.
read: Reported in NZD; a smaller deficit than forecast is read as better.
The deficit as a share of GDP is watched for vulnerability.
Usually low impact.
market: Smaller deficit → mildly supportive for NZD.
A large deficit can weigh on NZD over time.

name: RBNZ Survey of Expectations
freq: Quarterly, released shortly before the Monetary Policy Statement
what: The RBNZ surveys business leaders and economists on their expectations for inflation, wages, GDP and other variables. The 2-year-ahead inflation expectation is the most watched figure, because the RBNZ wants expectations anchored near 2%.
read: Focus on the 2-year inflation expectation versus the previous survey.
Expectations moving away from 2% signal a risk to the RBNZ's target.
Released close to RBNZ decisions, so it can shape the decision outlook.
market: Higher expectations → higher OCR expectations → NZD tends to rise.
Lower expectations → NZD tends to fall.

name: Global Dairy Trade Price Index
freq: Twice a month, at the end of an online auction (usually Tuesday, overnight New Zealand time)
what: Global Dairy Trade runs online auctions for dairy products such as whole milk powder and butter. Dairy is New Zealand's largest goods export, so dairy prices affect farm incomes and the economy.
read: Reported as the percentage change in the price index from the previous auction.
Whole milk powder prices matter most for New Zealand farm incomes.
Consecutive gains or falls show a trend; one auction can be noisy.
There is usually no consensus forecast.
market: Higher dairy prices → stronger export incomes → NZD tends to rise.
Falling dairy prices → NZD tends to weaken.
Impact is usually modest and seen in NZD/USD.

name: ANZ Business Outlook Survey
freq: Monthly, usually at the end of the month, 1:00 pm New Zealand time
what: ANZ surveys New Zealand businesses about their expectations for the economy, their own activity, prices and costs. Business confidence is the headline; own activity and pricing intentions give more detail.
read: Net balance: above zero means more firms are optimistic than pessimistic.
Own activity outlook often tracks the economy better than headline confidence.
Pricing intentions and inflation expectations are watched by the RBNZ.
No common consensus forecast; compare with the previous month.
market: Rising confidence → stronger growth outlook → mildly supportive for NZD.
Falling confidence → mildly negative.
Price expectations can shift OCR expectations.

name: BusinessNZ Performance of Manufacturing and Services Indexes
freq: Monthly, about 2 weeks after the month ends
what: BusinessNZ's Performance of Manufacturing Index (PMI) and Performance of Services Index (PSI) survey firms about production, orders, employment and inventories. They give an early read on activity.
read: Above 50 means expansion; below 50 means contraction.
Services matter more to the economy; manufacturing is more volatile.
No widely used consensus; compare with the prior reading.
market: Higher index → stronger growth outlook → mildly supportive for NZD.
Lower index → mildly negative.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Building Consents
freq: Monthly, about 4 weeks after the month ends, 10:45 am New Zealand time
what: Building consents count new dwellings approved for construction. They are a leading indicator of residential construction activity.
read: Volatile due to apartment and townhouse consents.
Annual totals show the trend more reliably.
Interest rates affect consents with a lag.
market: More consents → stronger construction outlook → mildly supportive for NZD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Producers Price Index
freq: Quarterly, about 7 weeks after the quarter ends, 10:45 am New Zealand time
what: The PPI measures changes in prices of inputs used by producers and outputs they sell. It is a lead indicator of cost pressures.
read: Higher than forecast suggests more pipeline inflation.
Input prices react to oil and import prices.
Usually low impact.
market: Higher producer prices → higher inflation outlook → mildly supportive for NZD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: International Visitor Arrivals
freq: Monthly, about 5–6 weeks after the month ends
what: The number of overseas visitors arriving in New Zealand. Tourism is a significant export of services.
read: Higher arrivals indicate stronger tourism exports.
Seasonal swings are large.
Usually low impact.
market: More visitors → mildly supportive for NZD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Bank of Canada Interest Rate Decision
freq: 8 times a year at 9:45 am Eastern time
what: The Bank of Canada's Governing Council sets the target for the overnight rate, Canada's main policy rate. Its goal is to keep inflation at the 2% midpoint of a 1–3% control range. The rate statement explains the decision and the outlook.
read: Decision versus forecast causes the largest moves; markets often price it in advance.
When unchanged, the statement's guidance on future moves matters most.
Look for changes in phrases about inflation risks and economic slack.
market: Higher rate or hawkish tone → CAD tends to strengthen.
Cut or dovish tone → CAD tends to weaken.
USD/CAD, CAD crosses and Canadian 2-year yields react first.
Oil prices and US rates also drive CAD on the same day.

name: Monetary Policy Report
freq: Quarterly (January, April, July, October), with the rate decision at 9:45 am Eastern time
what: The Monetary Policy Report contains the Bank of Canada's projections for inflation and growth and its view of the risks. It is released with four of the eight rate decisions.
read: Compare new inflation and GDP forecasts with the previous report.
Forecasts of inflation returning to 2% sooner can mean lower rates.
Scenario analysis (for example on trade tariffs) shows the risks the Bank weighs.
market: Higher inflation projections → higher rate expectations → CAD tends to rise.
Weaker growth or lower inflation projections → CAD tends to fall.
Combined with the rate decision reaction.

name: Bank of Canada Press Conference
freq: After each rate decision, at 10:30 am Eastern time
what: The Governor and Senior Deputy Governor explain the decision and answer journalists' questions. An opening statement is published at the start.
read: No number; markets read the tone.
Look for hints on the next move and on how the Bank sees risks.
Answers can differ in tone from the written statement.
market: Hawkish remarks → CAD tends to rise; dovish → CAD tends to fall.
USD/CAD reacts most.

name: Summary of Governing Council Deliberations
freq: About two weeks after each rate decision, 1:30 pm Eastern time
what: A summary of the discussion among Governing Council members before their last rate decision, including the arguments they weighed and the options considered.
read: No number; read the tone.
Look at whether members discussed different rate options.
Language on future decisions matters most.
market: More hawkish than expected → CAD tends to rise; more dovish → CAD tends to fall.
Reaction is usually smaller than on decision day.

name: Business Outlook Survey
freq: Quarterly, about 2 weeks before rate decisions in January, April, July and October, 10:30 am Eastern time
what: The Bank of Canada interviews about 100 businesses on their sales, investment, hiring, prices and inflation expectations. The headline Business Outlook Survey indicator summarises the results.
read: Higher indicator means stronger business sentiment.
Inflation expectations and price plans are watched closely.
It feeds into the Bank's next policy decision.
market: Stronger outlook → higher rate expectations → CAD tends to rise.
Weak outlook → CAD tends to fall.

name: Financial Stability Report
freq: Annually (May)
what: The Bank's assessment of risks to Canada's financial system, including household debt, housing and global risks.
read: No number; markets react only to policy signals.
Comments from the Governor at the release can matter.
market: Usually small impact on CAD.

name: Bank of Canada Officials' Speeches
freq: Irregular
what: The Governor, Senior Deputy Governor and Deputy Governors speak at events and testify before parliamentary committees. Their remarks can shift rate expectations between decisions.
read: The Governor's remarks carry the most weight.
Look for new views on inflation, growth or the next move.
Speeches with a press conference or Q&A can be more revealing.
market: Hawkish remarks → CAD tends to rise; dovish → CAD tends to fall.
USD/CAD and Canadian 2-year yields react most.

name: Labour Force Survey
freq: Monthly, usually the first Friday of the following month, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: The Labour Force Survey measures employment, unemployment and wages in Canada. It is often released the same day as the US jobs report, so USD/CAD can move sharply.
read: Employment change and unemployment rate are both watched; surprises in either move CAD.
Full-time versus part-time jobs show quality of hiring.
Average hourly wages of permanent employees signal wage pressure.
Monthly sampling noise is large; trend matters.
market: More jobs or lower unemployment → higher rate expectations → CAD tends to rise.
Weak jobs → CAD tends to fall.
When released with US payrolls, the gap between the two reports drives USD/CAD.

name: Consumer Price Index
freq: Monthly, around the third week of the following month, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: The CPI measures changes in prices paid by consumers. The Bank of Canada targets 2% CPI inflation. CPI-trim and CPI-median are the Bank's preferred core measures because they remove extreme price changes.
read: CPI-trim and CPI-median often matter more than headline CPI.
Compare y/y with the 2% target and the 1–3% control range.
Headline can be distorted by gasoline prices and tax changes.
Monthly changes in core can signal a turning point.
market: Higher inflation → higher rate expectations → CAD tends to rise.
Lower inflation → CAD tends to weaken.
USD/CAD and Canadian 2-year yields react most.

name: Gross Domestic Product
freq: Monthly (about 2 months after the month), quarterly with the third month, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: Statistics Canada publishes GDP by industry every month and expenditure-based GDP each quarter. Each monthly release also includes an advance estimate for the following month.
read: Monthly GDP change versus forecast is the headline.
The advance estimate for the next month can matter as much as the actual.
Quarterly releases are often shown as annualised growth.
Revisions can be important.
market: Stronger growth → higher rate expectations → CAD tends to rise.
Weak growth → CAD tends to fall.
USD/CAD reacts most.

name: Retail Trade
freq: Monthly, about 7 weeks after the month ends, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: Retail Trade measures the value of sales at Canadian retailers. Core retail sales exclude gasoline stations and motor vehicle and parts dealers. An advance estimate for the next month is included.
read: Core retail sales often give a better trend than headline.
Sales are in value terms; volume figures strip out price changes.
The advance estimate for the next month also moves markets.
market: Stronger sales → stronger growth outlook → CAD tends to rise.
Weak sales → CAD tends to fall.

name: International Merchandise Trade
freq: Monthly, about 5 weeks after the month ends, 8:30 am Eastern time (same time as US trade data)
what: The trade balance is the value of exported minus imported goods. Energy exports, especially crude oil to the United States, make the balance sensitive to oil prices and US demand.
read: A larger surplus or smaller deficit than forecast is read as better.
Energy prices and US tariffs strongly affect results.
Usually moderate impact.
market: Better balance → mildly supportive for CAD.
Weak exports → mildly negative.
Oil prices often matter more than the release.

name: Ivey Purchasing Managers Index
freq: Monthly, early in the following month, 10:00 am Eastern time
what: The Ivey PMI surveys purchasing managers about the dollar value of purchases compared with the previous month. It is an early indicator of economic activity in Canada.
read: Above 50 means more activity than the month before; below 50 means less.
ForexFactory shows the seasonally adjusted index.
Price sub-index hints at inflation pressure.
Readings can be volatile.
market: Higher PMI → stronger growth outlook → CAD tends to rise.
Lower PMI → CAD tends to weaken.
Reaction is usually modest.

name: Housing Starts
freq: Monthly, mid-month, 8:15 am Eastern time
what: The number of new housing units on which construction started, reported at an annualised rate. It reflects residential construction activity.
read: Higher than forecast means more construction activity.
Multi-unit starts make it volatile.
Interest rates affect it with a lag.
market: More starts → mildly supportive for CAD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Manufacturing and Wholesale Sales
freq: Monthly, about 6–7 weeks after the month ends, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: Monthly surveys of sales by manufacturers and wholesalers. They feed into GDP estimates. Statistics Canada also publishes flash estimates before the full release.
read: Higher than forecast is positive for growth.
Sales are in value terms; volume figures strip out price changes.
Flash estimates reduce surprises.
market: Stronger sales → mildly supportive for CAD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Building Permits
freq: Monthly, about 6 weeks after the month ends, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: The value of building permits issued by municipalities. It is a leading indicator of construction.
read: Very volatile due to large projects.
Residential and non-residential parts can diverge.
market: More permits → mildly supportive for CAD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Industrial Product and Raw Materials Price Indexes
freq: Monthly, about 3–4 weeks after the month ends, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: The IPPI measures prices received by manufacturers; the RMPI measures prices paid for raw materials. They follow energy and commodity prices and can point to future consumer inflation.
read: Higher than forecast means more pipeline inflation.
Energy prices drive most of the variation.
Usually low impact.
market: Higher producer prices → mildly supportive for CAD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Balance of International Payments: Current Account
freq: Quarterly, about 2 months after the quarter ends, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: The current account records trade in goods and services and investment income flows between Canada and the rest of the world.
read: Value in CAD; a smaller deficit or larger surplus is read as better.
Usually low impact.
market: Better balance → mildly supportive for CAD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: International Transactions in Securities
freq: Monthly, about 7 weeks after the month ends, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: This measures net foreign investment in Canadian stocks, bonds and money market securities. Large inflows mean foreigners are buying Canadian assets.
read: Positive means net foreign buying of Canadian securities.
Large swings often come from bond flows.
Usually low impact.
market: Larger inflows → more demand for CAD → mildly supportive.
Reaction is usually small.

name: Labour Productivity
freq: Quarterly, about 2 months after the quarter ends, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: Measures real output per hour worked in Canadian businesses. Productivity growth allows wages to rise without adding to inflation.
read: Higher than forecast is positive for the economy.
Low productivity with strong wages raises inflation concerns.
Usually low impact.
market: Stronger productivity → mildly supportive for CAD.
Reaction is usually small.

name: New Housing Price Index
freq: Monthly, about 3 weeks after the month ends, 8:30 am Eastern time
what: Measures changes in prices builders charge for new homes. It indicates housing market strength.
read: Higher than forecast means a firmer housing market.
Usually low impact.
market: Higher prices → mildly supportive for CAD.
Reaction is usually small.
